sights.name: Palazzo del Lavoro
sights.blurb: A giant square hall roofed by 16 freestanding concrete "mushroom" columns with steel umbrella caps. The glass and metal façades are rusting and broken. It is the southern gateway to the city.
sights.when: Owned through the CDP (Cassa Depositi e Prestiti) group; sources differ on the exact entity and date. Safety works were completed in early 2025. A shopping-centre plan was dropped. A rumoured Qatari cultural investment (Al Mayassa Al-Thani, ~€500M) reached "stallo" by April 2026.
sights.q: Palazzo del Lavoro, Via Ventimiglia 211, Torino

sights.name: Torino Esposizioni
sights.blurb: Nervi's 1948–50 prefabricated ferrocement vault, the "cattedrale moderna", plus Morandi's 1959 underground hall. It has been restored by Rafael Moneo with Isolarchitetti.
sights.when: Opening date repeatedly slipped (30 June 2026, then "autumn"). Presenting "Vale", the new Valentino cultural hub, Mayor Lo Russo announced 11 December 2026 as the public opening, with programming starting in November (Exibart). Not open on 20 Oct 2026.
sights.q: Torino Esposizioni, Corso Massimo d'Azeglio 15, Torino

sights.name: Lingotto: Pista 500 rooftop track
sights.blurb: The 1920s Fiat factory's rooftop banked test track, 28 m up. It is now a planted art garden (about 6,000 m², about 40,000 plants), with Renzo Piano's "Bolla" and "Scrigno" additions.
sights.when: Pinacoteca Agnelli is open Tue–Sun 10:00–19:00 (schedule valid 21 Sept–28 Oct 2026). Per Turismo Torino (the official tourist board), the Pinacoteca + Pista 500 combo costs €12 full / €8 reduced, and the Pista 500 alone €4 full / €2 reduced.

sights.name: Santo Volto and Parco Dora
sights.blurb: A brick church of seven 35 m towers, by Mario Botta, on a former Fiat Ferriere steelworks site. The old steelworks chimney is kept inside a steel spiral as its bell-tower.
sights.when: Active parish, free, open around services. The park is public.
sights.q: Chiesa del Santo Volto, Via Val della Torre 11, Torino

sights.name: Cimitero Parco
sights.blurb: About 690,000 m² of rolling lawns. Artificial hillocks hide the concrete burial complexes, and simple slabs lie flush in the grass with the Alps behind.
sights.when: Municipal cemetery, free. Check opening hours on the comune site.

sights.name: Piazza Risorgimento air-raid shelter
sights.blurb: Three parallel reinforced-concrete galleries about 40 m long and 4.5 m wide, 12 m underground, with 80 cm walls. Wartime rules of conduct are still painted on the walls. The access turrets have murals by XEL.
sights.when: Only on special openings. These include Museo Diffuso della Resistenza tours, FAI days and Monumenti Aperti (one edition ran Sat–Sun 10–12 and 14:30–16). Book through the Museo Diffuso (011 01120780).

sights.name: Corso Taranto IACP housing
sights.blurb: Sixteen eight-storey heavy-prefab slabs (652 flats) lined up on the heliothermic axis, designed by Nello Renacco. These are Turin's nearest analogue to a Falowiec or Aillaud estate in spirit, though not in scale.

sights.name: Chiesa del Gesù Redentore
sights.blurb: Bare brick walls under a faceted exposed reinforced-concrete vault, with a single nave.
sights.when: Active parish. The roof was restored in 2002.
sights.q: Chiesa Gesù Redentore, Piazza Giovanni XXIII 26, Torino

sights.name: Torre BBPR (Reale Mutua tower)
sights.blurb: A brick-clad "post-rationalist/brutalist" tower with oriel bays and porticoes, Milan-school neo-liberty. It is Turin's cousin of the Torre Velasca.

sights.name: Nietzsche's last lodging
sights.blurb: A marble plaque on the façade. His room was the fifth window from the corner, on the 4th floor, above the Galleria Subalpina entrance.
sights.when: Street plaque, always visible. The flat is private.

sights.name: Palazzo Campana
sights.blurb: A grand palazzo with a university entrance.
sights.when: University building. The courtyard is usually accessible in term time.
sights.q: Palazzo Campana, Via Carlo Alberto 10, Torino

sights.name: Cannonballs embedded in façades
sights.blurb: Iron shot from the 1706 siege and the 1799 fighting, walled into façades as memorials: two in the Palazzo Saluzzo Paesana courtyard (Via della Consolata 1 bis), more on Piazza San Carlo, Piazza Palazzo di Città and the Consolata.
sights.when: Public façades. Palazzo Saluzzo Paesana's courtyard is reachable during business hours.

sights.name: Fetta di Polenta
sights.blurb: A many-storey wedge-shaped house whose narrow end is 54 cm wide. Built by the Mole's architect.
sights.when: Private building, view from the street.
sights.q: Casa Scaccabarozzi, Via Giulia di Barolo 9, Torino

sights.name: Caffè Mulassano
sights.blurb: A 31 m² Liberty-style café, a Locale Storico d'Italia since 1985. Inside, a plaque reads "Nel 1926, la signora Angela Demichelis Nebiolo, inventò il tramezzino". The name is attributed to D'Annunzio, and sources give 1925 or 1926.
sights.when: Open, roughly 09:30–20:00 (to 19:30 Tue/Wed per TripAdvisor). It is classed as B (a "first"), not C.

sights.name: Palazzo Carignano
sights.blurb: Guarini's undulating brick baroque façade.
sights.q: Palazzo Carignano, Via Accademia delle Scienze 5, Torino

sights.name: Piazza San Carlo 2017 plaque
sights.blurb: A plaque placed in 2019 for the victims of the panic during the Juventus Champions League final screening, which was triggered by a robbery gang using pepper spray. Three people eventually died.

sights.name: "Baci Urbani"
sights.blurb: An oversized metal "piercing" ring stuck into the corner of an 18th-century building. It was meant as a temporary art installation and never removed.

sights.name: Ristorante Del Cambio
sights.blurb: Regional tourism site Piemonteitalia: "Nella sala più ampia è conservato il tavolo dove sedeva abitualmente il Conte Camillo Benso di Cavour". Rolling Stone Italia: "Il suo tavolo è ancora segnato con una targa commemorativa".
sights.when: Open, Michelin one star. Dinner roughly 19:30–23:30, Sunday lunch, plus a bistro at lunch. You can ask for Cavour's table when booking. Expensive; check delcambio.it.
sights.q: Ristorante Del Cambio, Piazza Carignano 2, Torino

sights.name: Caffè Elena
sights.blurb: Comune di Torino: "oggi si può fare colazione dove Cesare Pavese trascorreva il proprio tempo a scrivere". The original red breccia-marble tables survive. Giuseppe Carpano is said to have perfected his vermouth here in 1889–1902.
sights.when: Open. Mon–Fri 08–00, closed Wednesday; Sat 09–01; Sun 09–00 (official site).
sights.q: Caffè Elena, Piazza Vittorio Veneto 5, Torino

sights.name: Caffè Fiorio
sights.blurb: Frequented by Rattazzi, D'Azeglio, Balbo, Santorre di Santarosa and Cavour, who is said to have founded the Whist Club here.
sights.when: No closure reported. Check hours. Ignore one guide's wrong address (Piazza Castello 29).

sights.name: Al Bicerin
sights.blurb: By long tradition, Cavour drank here while waiting for the royal family to leave the Consolata sanctuary; one source frames it as "legend has it". Names on the wall (Dumas, Puccini, Nietzsche, Gozzano, Calvino) are tradition.
sights.when: Open, closed Wednesdays. About 08:30–19:30 (sources vary). Tiny, so expect a queue.
sights.q: Al Bicerin, Piazza della Consolata 5, Torino

sights.name: Caffè San Carlo
sights.blurb: A Risorgimento patriots' café (D'Azeglio, Cavour, Rattazzi, Giolitti, Crispi), closed several times for suspected subversion. A 1920s literary circle met here.
sights.when: Open, roughly 08:00–00:00. Management has changed several times, and it was closed for restoration 1953–63.
sights.q: Caffè San Carlo, Piazza San Carlo 156, Torino

sights.name: Caffè Platti
sights.blurb: Popular sources: Luigi Einaudi, Cesare Pavese, Natalia Ginzburg, and the founders of Fiat and Lavazza.
sights.when: Changed owner in Sept 2026. Gerla 1927 sold it to Villa Cimena Luxury Events (Balma family) through a new company, Platti il Salotto del Gusto S.r.l. Closed from about 1 Oct 2026 for restyling.
sights.q: Caffè Platti, Corso Vittorio Emanuele II 72, Torino

sights.name: Biblioteca Reale (Royal Library)
sights.when: Tourists see the Salone with a Musei Reali ticket, Mon and Fri 9:00–13:30 and Tue, Thu and Sat 13:30–18:30; currently it also hosts "Margherita, prima Regina d'Italia" until 6 Jan 2027.

sights.name: Accademia delle Scienze library
sights.blurb: Lagrange was a founder. Early members included Monge, Laplace, d'Alembert and Euler. It holds Coronelli globes.
sights.when: "Esclusivamente su appuntamento", Mon–Thu 9–13 and 15–17, Fri 9–13, through a form. Casual visitors usually get in only during events or conferences.
sights.q: Accademia delle Scienze, Via Maria Vittoria 3, Torino

sights.name: Teatro Regio (Mollino)
sights.blurb: Mollino's brick-and-concrete shell (built 1967–73) beside Juvarra's State Archive façade: foyers, the oval hall, and backstage workshops on the tour.
sights.when: 'Il Regio dietro le quinte' tours: Sat 15:00 and 16:30, Sun 11:00, 1 h, €10, Italian only, max 25. Tickets online from the Monday before each month's first tour.

sights.name: Palazzo degli Affari (Mollino)
sights.blurb: Chamber of Commerce block raised on a central core, a four-storey 'blade' linked by an aerial walkway, and Mollino's helical stair (1964–73).
sights.when: Working public offices; walk into the lobby in office hours. Occasional paid tours (Fondazione per l'architettura).
sights.q: Camera di Commercio, Via San Francesco da Paola 24, Torino

sights.name: Ex Borsa Valori
sights.blurb: Gabetti, Isola and Raineri's 1952–56 trading hall with its vaulted concrete roof, facing Piazzale Valdo Fusi. Closed since trading ended in 1992.
sights.when: Exterior only. Conversion planned: works may start 2028, finish 2030.
sights.q: Ex Borsa Valori, Via San Francesco da Paola 28, Torino

sights.name: Palazzo Nuovo (university)
sights.blurb: The hulking humanities slab (late 1960s–1970): one of Turin's first all-steel buildings, a steel frame behind glass walls rather than concrete, and criticised since it went up for pushing into the historic centre.
sights.when: Open in university hours; expect closures during protests (occupied 28 Jan–2 Feb 2026).

sights.name: Casa dell'Obelisco (Jaretti & Luzi)
sights.blurb: Undulating, banded 'litocemento' façades and an oyster-shaped entrance (1954–59): the provocative icon of Turin Neoliberty.

sights.name: Torri Pitagora (Jaretti & Luzi)
sights.blurb: Two ten-storey towers hollowed at the base into a 'forest of pillars', growing heavier as they rise (1962–68).
sights.when: Private, exterior only; Open House has offered interior visits.

sights.name: Falchera (Astengo's INA-Casa village)
sights.blurb: Turin's first INA-Casa satellite (1951–60): red-brick blocks on a hexagonal grid around a civic centre with a mushroom column. Falchera Nuova's 1970s towers stand just north.
sights.when: Public streets. Fondazione per l'architettura runs occasional guided walks.

sights.name: Le Vallette estate
sights.blurb: 71 ha of 1958–68 public housing by 45 architects (Gabetti & Isola, Levi Montalcini and others): towers, slabs and 'Scandinavian' courts. Gabetti & Isola's school is at Via dei Mughetti 26.
sights.when: Public streets; local history centre runs Open House tours.
sights.q: Piazza Eugenio Montale, Le Vallette, Torino

sights.name: San Paolo Apostolo
sights.blurb: Mario Bianco's all-concrete central plan (1967–69): a complex roof on massive pillars that seems to float above a ribbon of glass.
sights.when: Active parish; go around Mass times.
sights.q: Chiesa San Paolo Apostolo, Via Michele Berrino 12, Torino

sights.name: Santa Teresa di Gesù Bambino
sights.blurb: Post-conciliar church whose bell tower and roof dominate the local skyline (1961–70); OAT 2010 award.
sights.q: Chiesa Santa Teresa di Gesù Bambino, Via Giovanni da Verrazzano 48, Torino

sights.name: Gesù Operaio
sights.blurb: Felice Bardelli's 1963–67 church (he co-designed Palazzo Nuovo), with a gym in the undercroft; the census flags its structural system.
sights.when: Active parish. Exposed concrete unconfirmed; check in person.
sights.q: Chiesa Gesù Operaio, Via Leoncavallo 18, Torino

sights.name: San Luca Evangelista
sights.blurb: Roggero's 1967–71 church among the Mirafiori Sud public housing; also a MITO concert venue.
sights.when: Mass Sat 18:15, Sun 9:30/11/18:15. Exposed concrete unconfirmed.
sights.q: Chiesa San Luca Evangelista, Via Celeste Negarville 14, Torino

sights.name: San Michele Arcangelo
sights.blurb: Dolci and Tripodi's 1967–70 church with a pointed 'cuspide' roof, a short walk from Falchera.
sights.q: Chiesa San Michele Arcangelo, Corso Vercelli 390, Torino

sights.name: San Francesco di Sales
sights.blurb: Mario Bianco's 1973–78 church, by the designer of San Paolo Apostolo.
sights.when: Active parish. Materials and pin unverified.
sights.q: Chiesa San Francesco di Sales, Via Malta 42, Torino

sights.name: Santa Maria Goretti
sights.blurb: Modest 1964–67 church by Carbonara and Berardo in Parella.
sights.q: Chiesa Santa Maria Goretti, Via Vittorio Actis 20, Torino

sights.name: Italia '61 monorail stumps
sights.blurb: 14 of the 58 spans of the 1961 Alweg monorail viaduct on inverted-pyramid concrete piers, plus the south station shell, by the lake.
sights.when: Public park, always visible. Graffiti, spalling concrete, rough sleepers.
sights.q: Parco Italia 61, Corso Unità d'Italia, Torino

sights.name: Italia '61 illuminated fountain
sights.blurb: The original 1961 illuminated fountain near the Palavela, 'still there, though left to itself'.

sights.name: Monorail north station (Casa UGI)
sights.blurb: The 1961 north station, now a home for families of children with cancer.
sights.when: In use; exterior only, be discreet.
sights.q: Casa UGI, Corso Unità d'Italia 70, Torino

sights.name: Olympic arch and footbridge
sights.blurb: The 69 m red arch and the cable-stayed footbridge over the railway (2003–05), from the 1932 market arcades to the coloured athletes' village.
sights.when: Footbridge public; parts of ex-MOI vacant or fenced.
sights.q: Passerella Olimpica, Via Giordano Bruno, Torino

sights.name: Trincerone (sunken rail corridor)
sights.blurb: A 5.5 km sunken ex-rail corridor, overgrown and dumped in, seen from bridges and street edges.
sights.when: Time-sensitive: Metro 2 works start in the first half of 2027. View from public streets only.

sights.name: OSI-Ghia ruins
sights.blurb: A 1960 coachbuilding plant, abandoned since 2001.
sights.when: Fenced, exterior only; local press advises avoiding the area.

sights.name: ThyssenKrupp steelworks
sights.blurb: Vast vacant sheds of the steelworks where seven workers died in the December 2007 fire.
sights.when: Fenced, exterior only. Visit with respect.

sights.name: Ex-Superga factory
sights.blurb: Sheds of the plant where the canvas sneaker was made, abandoned since 1998.
sights.when: Exterior only; becoming a Paratissima culture hub (about three years of works).

sights.name: Officine Grandi Motori
sights.blurb: Fiat's 1911 'Basilica' hall and the 'Lingottino', shells on a fenced demolition and clean-up site.
sights.when: Time-sensitive: works since Feb 2025; view from Corso Vigevano.
sights.q: Officine Grandi Motori, Corso Vigevano, Torino

sights.name: Le Nuove prison shelter
sights.blurb: An air-raid shelter 18 m deep inside the 19th-century prison, told through political and Jewish prisoners' testimony.
sights.when: Guided only, booking required (011 7604881): 25 places, about 1 h 15, €8 / €5, Abbonamento Musei valid.
sights.q: Museo del Carcere Le Nuove, Via Paolo Borsellino 3, Torino

sights.name: Palazzo Civico air-raid shelter
sights.blurb: A 1940 shelter 10 m under the town hall's courtyard: 20 × 3 m for 50 staff, rusting gas-tight doors and original wall signs.
sights.when: Free visits since 2017; current schedule not found.
sights.q: Palazzo Civico, Piazza Palazzo di Città 1, Torino

sights.name: Mirafiori shelter and Chiesa della Visitazione
sights.blurb: A 1934 concrete church with crypt, and the shelter that protected the Mirafiori borgo, on a 90-minute tour from the lost Savoy castle site.
sights.when: No tour dates bookable now; watch arteemusei.com.
sights.q: Chiesa della Visitazione, Strada Castello di Mirafiori 42, Torino

sights.name: PalaRuffini (Vitellozzi)
sights.blurb: Vitellozzi's 1959–61 concrete arena for Italia '61, twin of his Rome Palazzetto; his own favourite.
sights.when: Exterior always visible in Parco Ruffini; inside on match days (Basket Torino).

sights.name: Fiat Mirafiori: Palazzina and Corso Tazzoli
sights.blurb: The 220 m white-stone office block (1937–39) and a clinker front almost 1 km long on Corso Tazzoli; Porta 5 was the gate of the 1970s labour struggles.
sights.when: Private; view from the pavements. The Palazzina reopens as a campus by 2027, so expect works.

sights.name: Tempio Crematorio and Luogo del Ricordo
sights.blurb: Italy's second crematorium (1882) with Cordero sculptures in its modern garden, and the city's ash-scattering garden of three fountains over Luserna stone.

sights.name: Palazzo di Giustizia
sights.blurb: A 300 m courthouse (1990–2000) in brick and 30,000 m² of glass: megastructure scale, not concrete.
sights.q: Palazzo di Giustizia, Corso Vittorio Emanuele II 130, Torino

sights.name: Santi Apostoli, Piossasco
sights.blurb: Gabetti & Isola's church built from prefab factory-shed parts (1969–73): 24 m concrete trusses, U-glass walls, a giant precast cross. Built for Fiat Rivalta workers.
sights.when: Active parish, open around Mass. Car or bus; pair with Collegno.
sights.q: Chiesa Santi Apostoli, Via Pinerolo 161, Piossasco

sights.name: San Pietro in Vincoli, Moriondo
sights.blurb: Nicola Mosso's pentagonal church: six exposed pillars, a roof broken into triangles, light through the gaps. A sibling of the Redentore.
sights.q: Chiesa San Pietro in Vincoli, Via Duca d'Aosta 3, Moncalieri

sights.name: SS. Trinità, Nichelino
sights.blurb: Pratesi's 1970–73 church: exposed concrete beams knitting into a net, modelled on the Redentore. Roof leaks and decaying concrete.
sights.when: Active parish (Via Stupinigi 16); check the pin.
sights.q: Parrocchia SS. Trinità, Via Stupinigi 16, Nichelino

sights.name: FATA HQ, Pianezza (Niemeyer + Morandi)
sights.blurb: Niemeyer and Morandi's 1976–79 'land bridge': a 100 m office block hung from great arches, with 21.30 m cantilevers on six hollow piers.
sights.when: Company offices; photograph from the road, don't enter the grounds.

sights.name: Collegno: Certosa and ex-asylum
sights.blurb: A 17th-century charterhouse that became the Royal asylum in 1852; walls down after 1978, now a park of 40 ha with some abandoned pavilions.
sights.when: Park open daily; free visits with the Ciceroni Collegnesi. Pavilions not visitable.
sights.q: Certosa Reale, Via Martiri XXX Aprile 30, Collegno

sights.name: Casa Martini, Pessione
sights.blurb: The wine museum in the 18th-century cellars of the first Martini & Rossi plant (1864), with stills and presses.
sights.q: Casa Martini, Piazza Luigi Rossi 2, Pessione

sights.name: 1864 bullet dent, Caval ëd Bronz
sights.blurb: A bullet dent on the Cateau-Cambrésis bas-relief of the equestrian statue, from the night of 22 September 1864.
sights.when: Always visible; look at the plinth reliefs.
sights.q: Monumento a Emanuele Filiberto, Piazza San Carlo, Torino

sights.name: Rondò della Forca: Cafasso monument
sights.blurb: A 1960 bronze of the 'gallows priest' Cafasso, on the spot where public hangings were held 1835–1853.
sights.q: Rondò della Forca, Corso Regina Margherita, Torino

sights.name: Piazza Carlina: guillotine square
sights.blurb: No marker: under French rule (1798–1814) the guillotine stood about where Cavour's statue is; 423 executions reported. Gramsci's 1919–21 lodging plaque is at no. 15.

sights.name: Sacrario del Martinetto
sights.blurb: The small rifle range where RSI firing squads shot about sixty partisans in 1943–45; a stone post and a plaque with 59 names.
sights.when: Memorial site; check access times with the Museo Diffuso.
sights.q: Sacrario del Martinetto, Corso Svizzera, Torino

sights.name: Pian del Lot memorial
sights.blurb: Granite monument where 27 prisoners from Le Nuove were shot on 2 April 1944; the first municipal plaque on the back still shows doubt about some names.
sights.when: Outdoor, always open; car or bus up the Maddalena road.
sights.q: Sacrario Pian del Lot, Strada Comunale di Pian del Lot, Torino

sights.name: Via Cibrario 1: 'in questo luogo'
sights.blurb: The plaque on the exact spot where nine partisans, two of them unknown Frenchmen, were shot on 12 October 1944. Another for nine shot stands on Piazza Statuto.

sights.name: Piazza XVIII Dicembre plaque (1922)
sights.blurb: Plaque for the 18–20 December 1922 Fascist massacre: 11 killed by Brandimarte's squads, the Camera del Lavoro burned. A second plaque is in the metro station.

sights.name: Angelo Azzurro plaque (1977)
sights.blurb: Where Roberto Crescenzio, 22, died after militants firebombed the bar on 1 October 1977 believing it a neo-fascist haunt. Plaque 2017.
sights.when: Street plaque; the premises are a bar again.

sights.name: Corso Re Umberto 54: Casalegno
sights.blurb: The doorway where the Red Brigades shot La Stampa's deputy editor Carlo Casalegno on 16 November 1977; nothing on the street recalls it.

sights.name: Pietro Micca museum and siege tunnels
sights.blurb: Down to 6 and 14 m into the 1706 counter-mine galleries, to the stair Pietro Micca ran down and the spot where his body was found.
sights.when: Tue–Sun 10–18; tunnel visits booked (011 01167580) at 10:30, 14:30, 16:30 (+15:30 Sun). Abbonamento Musei valid.
sights.q: Museo Pietro Micca, Via Guicciardini 7, Torino

sights.name: Mastio della Cittadella
sights.blurb: The surviving keep of the 1564 citadel, now the Artillery museum. Its front 'door' is a fake, topped by a grimacing mask to mock invaders.
sights.when: Opens for exhibitions; hours irregular. Exterior always visible.
sights.q: Mastio della Cittadella, Corso Galileo Ferraris 2, Torino

sights.name: Teatro di Torino ruin
sights.blurb: Perimeter walls and part of the foyer of the 1857 theatre gutted by bombs on 8 December 1942: 'the only conspicuous visible memory' of the war damage.
sights.when: Visible from the street, no entry.

sights.name: Piazza Valdo Fusi: the bombing void
sights.blurb: An open square over a car park where a whole city block, the old Politecnico, stood before the bombs.

sights.name: Synagogue and the walled-up door
sights.blurb: The Moorish-style synagogue, gutted in the 21 November 1942 raid with only its four towers standing; on Via Sant'Anselmo the old 'brides' door' at no. 7 is bricked up.
sights.when: Exterior always; interior by booking with the Jewish Community.
sights.q: Sinagoga, Via San Pio V 12, Torino

sights.name: Monte dei Cappuccini shelter mouths
sights.blurb: Eight WWII tunnel entrances in the hillside retaining wall, six bricked up: one of only two public shelters dug into the hill.
sights.when: Visible from the street, no entry.

sights.name: Parco Leopardi shelter entrances
sights.blurb: Four walled-up shelter mouths marked 'P.A.A.' (Protezione Anti Aerea).

sights.name: Porta Nuova deportation plaque
sights.blurb: 'Partirono da questa stazione i deportati politici per i campi di sterminio nazisti…'
sights.q: Stazione Porta Nuova, Via Sacchi, Torino

sights.name: Pietre d'inciampo, Via Po 25
sights.blurb: Stones for Michele Valabrega and Maria Irene Roscetti, deported on Primo Levi's convoy. Turin has 130: also Piazza Castello 161 (the Colombo family), Corso San Maurizio 8, Via San Domenico 0–1.

sights.name: Cascina Marchesa: Grandi Motori plaques
sights.blurb: Two relocated factory plaques; one marks where five worker-partisans fell under German tank fire on 27 April 1945.

sights.name: Museo Diffuso: rescued factory plaques
sights.blurb: Courtyard plaques taken from Fiat Ferriere and Grandi Motori ('…from which the first spark of the revolt…, 18–28 April 1945').
sights.q: Museo Diffuso della Resistenza, Corso Valdocco 4, Torino

sights.name: Superga: the Grande Torino crash wall
sights.blurb: The basilica's rear retaining wall, still marked by the 4 May 1949 impact that killed the Grande Torino team, with the marble plaque of victims.
sights.q: Lapide Grande Torino, Basilica di Superga, Torino

sights.name: Hotel Roma: Pavese's room 346
sights.blurb: The working hotel where Cesare Pavese was found dead in room 346 on 27 August 1950.
sights.q: Hotel Roma e Rocca Cavour, Piazza Carlo Felice 60, Torino

sights.name: Palazzo Cavour plaque
sights.blurb: 1861 marble: Cavour was born in this house on 10 August 1810 and died here on 6 June 1861.

sights.name: Cinema Statuto memorial
sights.blurb: A garden bed and plaque for the 64 who died behind chained exits in the fire of 13 February 1983, which led to Italy's cinema fire law.

sights.name: Arsenale: Paolo Sacchi plaque
sights.blurb: 1886 bronze for the sergeant who kept 40,000 kg of powder from exploding on 26 April 1852, when the magazine blast damaged every house in Borgo Dora.
sights.when: Always visible (now Sermig's Arsenale della Pace).
sights.q: Arsenale della Pace, Piazza Borgo Dora 61, Torino

sights.name: Rousseau's abjuration, Spirito Santo
sights.blurb: Where the 16-year-old Rousseau was registered at the Catecumeni hospice in April 1728 and abjured Calvinism. He later served as a footman in Palazzo Solaro (now MAO, Via San Domenico 11).
sights.q: Chiesa dello Spirito Santo, Via Porta Palatina 9, Torino

sights.name: Guglia Beccaria (geodetic baseline)
sights.blurb: The 1808 obelisk on the end-stone of Beccaria's 1760 baseline for measuring a degree of meridian. Its twin stands 11.8 km west at Rivoli. The black-magic stories are myth.

sights.name: Rivoli twin obelisk
sights.blurb: The western end of Beccaria's baseline, inaugurated 8 October 1808, with a 1934 plaque in the pavement by the newsstand at the start of Via Fratelli Piol.

sights.name: Sobrero nitroglycerine plaque
sights.blurb: 'In the old chemical laboratory of this building Ascanio Sobrero… first realised the synthesis of nitroglycerine' (1846–47). His monument is in the Valentino.

sights.name: Ex-Ospizio di Carità: 1896 Lumière show
sights.blurb: Where Vittorio Calcina showed about twenty Lumière shorts on 7 November 1896, in the former Ospizio di Carità at Via Po 33. It is often billed as Italy's first public film show, but Calcina had already shown the Lumière films in Milan on 29 March 1896, so treat "first" as disputed. What Turin can fairly claim is one of Italy's earliest permanent cinemas, opened here late in 1896.

sights.name: Old university, Via Po 17
sights.blurb: The 1714–20 university courtyard where Beccaria taught physics; the 1904 fire here burned the National Library's manuscripts and launched library chemistry.

sights.name: Palazzo Madama observatory tower
sights.blurb: The west tower held the city observatory 1822–1912 until electric lights ruined the sky; the dome went in 1920.
sights.when: Nothing left; look up at the tower.

sights.name: Ambrosio film studios
sights.blurb: Fenoglio's 1911–13 office block and glass-roofed stage of Italy's biggest silent-film studio, now Teatro Espace.

sights.name: Itala Film site
sights.blurb: Pastrone's studio behind Cabiria (1914), built 1906–15. Whether anything survives is unconfirmed.

sights.name: Cinema Nuovo Romano
sights.blurb: A working cinema in the 1870s Galleria Subalpina, with a Lumière room in the basement from 1905.

sights.name: Fiat's first plant, Corso Dante
sights.blurb: The 1899–1900 Fiat buildings, centre of the September 1920 factory occupations, bombed in 1942, now lofts.

sights.name: Palazzo Bricherasio
sights.blurb: Where Fiat's founding deed was signed in July 1899. No Fiat plaque outside (only one for the poet Berchet).

sights.name: Carpano vermouth plaque
sights.blurb: 'Nel 1786 in questa casa creò il suo Vermouth…' The shop is documented; inventing vermouth is tradition.
sights.q: Piazza Castello at Via Viotti, Torino

sights.name: Juventus founding bench
sights.blurb: A bench repainted black-and-white in July 2025 with a plaque, opposite where the club was founded in 1897; the original is in the J Museum.
sights.q: Corso Re Umberto at Corso Vittorio Emanuele II, Torino

sights.name: Bar Norman (Torino FC founded)
sights.blurb: Torino FC was founded on the mezzanine of the then Birreria Voigt on 3 December 1906; plaque and founders' photo inside.
sights.q: Bar Norman, Via Pietro Micca 22, Torino

sights.name: Michelin chimney, Parco Dora
sights.blurb: The stamping-shop chimney, all that is left of Michelin's first Italian plant (1906).

sights.name: Lagrange birthplace
sights.blurb: A faded plaque: Lagrange was born here on 25 January 1736. He later chaired the metric-system commission.

sights.name: Anatomy, Lombroso and Fruit museums
sights.blurb: Three 19th-century museums in one building: Rolando's anatomy rooms, Lombroso's criminal anthropology (discredited science, which is why it matters) and Garnier Valletti's artificial fruits.
sights.q: Museo Lombroso, Via Pietro Giuria 15, Torino

sights.name: Regia Farmacia Masino (1667)
sights.blurb: A pharmacy trading since 1667, with 18th-century fittings, jars and a bronze mortar of 1718.
sights.q: Farmacia Masino, Via Maria Vittoria 3, Torino

sights.name: Farmacia Anglesio
sights.blurb: In the same family since 1682: big historic sign and original fittings. The Farmacia della Consolata (Via delle Orfane 25) is nearby.

sights.name: L'Ordine Nuovo plaque
sights.blurb: 1949 plaque where Gramsci's L'Ordine Nuovo was written; later Einaudi's first offices.

sights.name: Teatro Nuovo: the march of the 40,000
sights.blurb: On 14 October 1980 a Fiat supervisors' meeting here overflowed into the silent march that ended the 35-day strike.
sights.q: Teatro Nuovo, Corso Massimo d'Azeglio 17, Torino

sights.name: Ex Capamianto asbestos factory
sights.blurb: 1911–1952 asbestos-factory buildings, 'of documentary interest' in the 1984 census.
sights.q: Corso Peschiera at Via Sant'Antonino, Torino

sights.name: Galileo Ferraris IEEE Milestone
sights.blurb: IEEE plaque for the rotating field and early induction motors (1885–88), dedicated 2021.
sights.when: Energy Center entrance hall; may have moved to the Politecnico (Sala Emma Strada).
sights.q: Energy Center, Via Paolo Borsellino 38, Torino

sights.name: Lavazza's first shop
sights.blurb: Luigi Lavazza's 1895 grocery where he began blending coffee, now a café with company photos.
sights.q: San Tommaso 10, Via San Tommaso 10, Torino

sights.name: Lancia's first workshop
sights.blurb: Founded 27 November 1906 at the corner of Via Ormea and Via Donizetti; the doors reportedly had to be widened to get the first car out.
sights.q: Via Ormea at Via Donizetti, Torino

sights.name: Aeritalia airfield: first airmail
sights.blurb: On 22 May 1917 De Bernardi flew the world's first airmail from the Pomilio field here to Rome. Still Aero Club Torino's field.

sights.name: University Botanic Garden
sights.blurb: The 1729 royal garden by the Valentino castle, with old Ginkgo, cedar and yew.
sights.when: Sat 14:30–19, Sun 10–19 late Mar–mid Nov, €5; closed for winter from ~17 Nov.

sights.when: Partly open; more works approved Oct 2026.

sights.name: Primo Levi's house
sights.blurb: Primo Levi's birth and death house; his surname still on the doorbell.

sights.name: SOMS Edmondo De Amicis
sights.blurb: A still-active workers' mutual-aid society club, with banners and members' photos on the walls.

sights.name: Renzi urinal, Piazza Villari
sights.blurb: A Liberty-era cast-stone urinal stamped 'U. Renzi', one of the two oldest of about 29 survivors, repainted in pastels as street art.

sights.name: Renzi urinal, Corso Massimo d'Azeglio

sights.name: Vanchiglia public baths (1901)
sights.blurb: A modest Liberty bathhouse by Dolza that still works as public baths, run by volunteers.

sights.name: Ex-bagni, Via Morgari (San Salvario)
sights.blurb: Dolza's Liberty bathhouse with curving wings and a cornice of alternating frogs and shells, now the Casa del Quartiere café.
sights.q: Casa del Quartiere di San Salvario, Via Morgari 14, Torino

sights.name: Ex-bagni of San Donato (1900)
sights.blurb: The district's first shower baths and wash-house with zoomorphic decoration, now a library.

sights.name: Via Agliè public baths (1956)
sights.blurb: A working 1956 bathhouse in Barriera di Milano that replaced baths in a demolished toll house.

sights.name: Via Cherasco public baths
sights.blurb: An early-20th-century bathhouse whose eight showers still run.

sights.name: 1912 toll house, Piazza Rebaudengo
sights.blurb: The yellow 1912 customs office of the northern gate, in its original form, with a flying-ship mural. The big 'barrier' squares exist because the gates stood there.

sights.name: Toll house, Piazza Stampalia
sights.blurb: 1912 toll quarters of the Barriera di Lanzo, now a district meeting centre.

sights.name: Toll house, Piazza Bengasi
sights.blurb: The 1912 customs house on the Moncalieri border, nearly lost to Metro 1 and restored in original colours in 2023.

sights.name: Ice-houses in the Mercato Centrale
sights.blurb: Two 19th-century underground ice chambers found in 2002, left open to view in a sunken plaza of Fuksas's market hall: domes, drainage floors, roof hatches.
sights.when: Free in building hours; layout changes, check.
sights.q: Mercato Centrale, Piazza della Repubblica 25, Torino

sights.name: Po flood column
sights.blurb: The column by the Borgo Medievale recording the great floods: highest October 1839 at 6.20 m; 2000 and 2016 within 30–50 cm.

sights.name: Museo dei Lavandai, Bertolla
sights.blurb: Turin's laundry village (1872–1960s): washing tools, the kneeling 'scagn', photos.
sights.q: Museo dei Lavandai, Strada Comunale di Bertolla 113, Torino

sights.name: Sassi–Superga rack tramway
sights.blurb: The 1884 line (a cable-hauled Agudio funicular at first, a rack railway since 1935) climbing 3.1 km at up to 21% in 1934 cars; Sassi station keeps a small history room.
sights.when: Hourly 10–18 from Sassi in season, no service Wed; winter suspensions. Check gtt.to.it.

sights.name: Ponte Mosca
sights.blurb: A single flat stone arch over the Dora, 45 m span and only 5.5 m rise (1823–30), 'a unicum' of early 19th-century stone bridges.
sights.when: Best from the Lungo Dora path.
sights.q: Ponte Mosca, Corso Giulio Cesare, Torino

sights.name: Old Torino–Ceres terminus
sights.blurb: The 1869 terminus of the Lanzo Valleys railway, disused since 1986.

sights.name: Duomo meridian line
sights.blurb: A noon line on the cathedral's side wall marking the zodiac, with a star-shaped gnomon: an ordinary sundial, not an anti-Church code.
sights.when: Go near solar noon (about 12:20, 13:20 in summer time).
sights.q: Duomo di Torino, Piazza San Giovanni, Torino

sights.name: Fountain of seven torèt
sights.blurb: Seven of Turin's 800 green bull-head fountains in a semicircle. The 'lovers' pair faces off at Via Stampatori 4.

sights.name: Brass bull of Piazza San Carlo
sights.blurb: The rearing bull set in the arcade pavement; spin on its testicles for luck.

sights.name: 'Columbus's finger'
sights.blurb: Students rub Columbus's finger for luck; the bronze is actually Somà's 1923 memorial to Latin-American Italian WWI volunteers.

sights.name: Frejus tunnel monument
sights.blurb: A pyramid of real rocks from the 1871 tunnel dig with Titans and a winged Genius of Science (1879). The 'Lucifer' is a legend.

sights.name: Portone del Diavolo
sights.blurb: A 1675 Parisian door with a gilded devil-head knocker. Same corner: the 'Horns of Pan' mask; more masks at Via Alfieri 15.
sights.when: Always visible; the ghosts are legend.

sights.name: Torre Littoria
sights.blurb: Turin's first 'grattanuvole' (1933–34, 87 m), meant as the Fascist HQ: 'il dito del Duce'. Its own plaque gives the wrong dates.

sights.name: T'oro: bull bursting from a wall
sights.blurb: Richi Ferrero's half bull with golden horns smashing out of brick.

sights.name: Upside-down David

sights.name: Lampioni innamorati bench
sights.blurb: An iron bench where two street lamps sit, one leaning on the other (Marasciuolo, 2002).

sights.blurb: The central section of a 1915–18 submarine, placed in the Valentino in 1933.
sights.q: Sommergibile Provana, Viale Marinai d'Italia, Torino

sights.name: Palace of the bats
sights.blurb: Two big stone bats under the third-floor balconies (1876).

sights.name: Smallest piazzetta
sights.blurb: About 17 × 13 m with its own sign and number; Cavour's funeral was held in its church.
sights.q: Piazzetta Beata Vergine degli Angeli, Torino

sights.blurb: About 23–30 m long with two house numbers on two mirror buildings. The narrowest, vicolo Santa Maria, is 2.85 m.

offmap.name: Cesana Pariol bobsleigh/luge track
offmap.blurb: A long zig-zag "serpentone" of concrete and sheet metal down a larch slope, with refrigeration plant and stands. It is the nearest thing in Italy to Sarajevo's Trebević track.
offmap.when: €9M has been allocated for (partial) demolition and "rinaturalizzazione".
offmap.q: Pista di bob Cesana Pariol, Cesana Torinese

offmap.name: Pragelato Olympic ski jumps
offmap.blurb: Five jumps (HS106 and HS140 Olympic hills), a judges' tower and an abandoned hotel at the foot. The jumps' green plastic summer matting is disintegrating, and one 2025 visitor called it an ecological "time bomb".
offmap.when: The area below the jumps is being converted for biathlon and roller-skiing (≈€5M, Universiade works, permanent facility targeted for winter 2026–27). The jumps themselves are being kept, not demolished ("troppo caro smontarli").

offmap.name: Ivrea
offmap.blurb: Talponia is a semicircular, half-buried "horizontal skyscraper" about 300 m long, with 82 duplex and simplex cells facing a hillside under a grass roof. Beyond it, the Via Jervis axis: Figini & Pollini's ICO works and social services, Gino Valle's offices, the open-air MaAM, and the all-concrete Sacro Cuore church (Favini structures).
offmap.when: Talponia is lived in, so walk past respectfully. UNESCO Visitor Centre, Via Jervis 11: free, Tue–Sun 10–18 until 15 Nov 2026; weekend tours at 10:00 and 15:00. ICO and the social-services building inside only on guided tours.

offmap.name: Mollino's Lago Nero sled station
offmap.blurb: Mollino's 1946–47 sled-lift station at 2,286 m above Sauze d'Oulx, restored 1999–2005, now a ski-season refuge.
offmap.when: On foot from Pian della Rocca via Sportinia in summer, by lifts in winter. Check the season (0122 858009).
offmap.q: Chalet Mollino, Lago Nero, Sauze d'Oulx

offmap.name: Forte di Fenestrelle
offmap.blurb: A fortress chain climbing the mountainside in Val Chisone, billed as Europe's longest fortification.
offmap.when: Guided only, booking by phone; routes 1, 3 or 7 h ('Passeggiata Reale' €20). Winter hours vary.

offmap.name: Forte di Exilles
offmap.blurb: A fortress of the Susa Valley, razed by the French in 1796 and rebuilt in 1818–29, with galleries and underground passages. It now houses the National Mountain Museum (guided tours).
offmap.when: Season 20 Jun–27 Sep; special opening 31 Oct 2026. Exterior visible from the SS24.

offmap.name: Orco dams: Ceresole and Serrù
offmap.blurb: Ceresole's gravity dam (built 1925–31) in Gran Paradiso park, with the Serrù and Agnel dams above 2,000 m on the Nivolet road, and the Rosone power station below.
offmap.when: Ceresole visible year-round; the high road closes in winter (summer 2027 target).

offmap.name: Mont-Cenis: dam and Vallo Alpino forts
offmap.blurb: A 120 m-high, 1.4 km-long embankment dam (EDF, 1962–69) whose reservoir is shared roughly 4/5 France and 1/5 Italy, and the 1933–42 Italian strongpoints of the Vallo Alpino around the pass: caves, firing posts, steel cupolas.
offmap.when: Summer only; forts entered entirely at your own risk (torch, stay on paths). French territory since 1947.

offmap.name: Valle Stura Vallo Alpino and Vinadio
offmap.blurb: Opera 5 'San Membotto' with the only mortar block on the western Alps, and the Forte di Vinadio's 'Caverna Comando'.
offmap.when: Trail-side works; Vinadio by guided route. A long day trip into Cuneo province.

offmap.blurb: An 1878 wool mill with its water-power transmission, machinery and 2 km of archives, on the Biella 'Strada della Lana'.
offmap.when: Summer Sundays 14:30–18:30 to end Oct, €5; after October by appointment (351 3902199).

p: You are looking at a square hall 158 metres on each side, roofed by sixteen giant concrete columns. Each one starts at the ground as a cross and tapers as it rises 25 metres into a round shaft, and on top of each sits a steel "umbrella" 40 metres across. The sixteen umbrellas don't quite touch, and the strips of glass between them let light fall into the hall. Today the glass and metal walls are rusting and broken, so from the street you can look straight into the forest of columns.

It was built for Italia '61, the great exhibition for the hundredth anniversary of Italian unification; Turin had been Italy's first capital in 1861. Pier Luigi Nervi, the greatest Italian engineer of the century, won the 1959 competition with his son Antonio. The steel was designed by Gino Covre, and Gio Ponti staged the opening show, the International Labour Exhibition, "Man at Work". The design was chosen partly because it could be built fast: each column and umbrella was an identical module, so the work could be repeated sixteen times. Queen Elizabeth II visited in 1961, and a monorail ran from here along the river to the north station.

After the exhibition it held a university faculty until about 2008, plus trade fairs, the odd disco, car showrooms and Torino FC's title parties. Then it was emptied. Arson fires in 2015 damaged it further, and plants have started to colonise the inside. It is listed, which protects it from demolition but has also made every reuse plan stall: a shopping centre was dropped, and a rumoured Qatari cultural investment of about €500M had stalled by April 2026. It is owned through the state lender CDP's property group (sources differ on the exact company and date).

It is fenced and structurally unsafe, so don't go in. Walk the perimeter on Corso Unità d'Italia and Via Ventimiglia: through the gaps you see the columns and the light on them, and the scale is hard to believe. It is the biggest and saddest of Turin's modern ruins. The monorail stumps and the 1961 fountain are a short walk away.
lavoro.s: CDP Real Asset; urbipedia; Politecnico di Torino theses; Torino Oggi (Apr 2026); CDP

p: Inside this unremarkable-looking exhibition complex on the edge of the Valentino park is one of the great rooms of modern engineering: Nervi's Hall B, about 96 by 75 metres, roofed by a single thin corrugated vault with no columns. The vault is made of ferrocement, Nervi's own invention: thin layers of cement over many layers of fine steel mesh, cast in small pieces on site and then assembled like a puzzle. The light comes in through the gaps in the corrugations.

The complex began in 1936 as Ettore Sottsass Sr.'s Palazzo della Moda. It was bombed in the war, and Turin's car industry wanted a showcase quickly. Nervi built the new hall in a few months and it opened on 15 September 1948 for the 31st Motor Show, advertised as "the most beautiful building Italy has ever built". It made him world-famous and tied him to Fiat; the Palazzo del Lavoro followed. In 1959 Riccardo Morandi added an underground hall. The Motor Show and the Book Fair were held here, the 2006 Olympics used it as an ice-hockey rink, and a car chase for *The Italian Job* (1969) was filmed here (it was cut from the final film).

Now it is being turned into Turin's new central library, restored by Rafael Moneo with Isolarchitetti, a roughly €166M project. Most of the new rooms are put underground so that the great hall stays one open space. The city gives 20,000 m² of floor space; the culture assessor quoted 24,000 m², 1,000 study seats and 150,000 books on open shelves. That would make it one of the largest public libraries in Italy.

The opening kept slipping. The mayor has announced 11 December 2026 as the public opening, with events from November; it was still closed on 20 October 2026. As a public library it should be free. Before then you see only the outside, from Corso Massimo d'Azeglio and the park. If you are in Turin after the opening, this is the stop to sit and read under Nervi's vault.
esposizioni.s: Domus (1948, archive); Laboratorio Nervi, Politecnico di Milano; Comune di Torino (Jul 2026); Quotidiano Piemontese; Exibart

p: High in the Val di Susa, a long concrete-and-metal track zig-zags down a larch-covered slope, with a refrigeration plant, empty stands and start houses. This is the bobsleigh, luge and skeleton track of the 2006 Winter Olympics. It is the nearest thing in Italy to Sarajevo's abandoned 1984 Olympic track on Mount Trebević: a piece of sport infrastructure built for two weeks of television and then left behind.

It cost €110M and seated 7,130 spectators. The South Tyrolean luger Armin Zöggeler never lost on it and won one of Italy's five home gold medals here. But a bob track needs to be refrigerated, staffed and maintained, and there are only a few hundred athletes in the sport. It lost €1.3–1.5M a year and closed around 2011–12. In 2023 Italy floated reviving it for the Milano-Cortina 2026 games; the IOC refused, pointing out that it had already been abandoned once, and Cortina built a new track instead, a decision that was itself controversial.

Turin's 2006 games left several such ruins in the valleys: this track, the Pragelato ski jumps, and an Olympic village in the city that ended up occupied. They are now a standard example in debates about the cost of hosting the Olympics.

Its days are numbered. €9M has been set aside for partial demolition and returning the slope to nature, and in 2025 the government commissioner said works would start in summer 2026. It was still standing in July 2026, and I found no report that work has begun. Expect fencing, and check local news (Luna Nuova, ValsusaOggi) before the trip. It's about 85 km from Turin; pair it with Pragelato in the next valley.
cesana.s: Eco del Chisone (Apr 2025); Luna Nuova; ValsusaOggi

p: Five ski jumps stand side by side above the village of Pragelato in Val Chisone, with a judges' tower beside them and an empty hotel at the foot. The two big ones are the Olympic hills of 2006. In summer you see the green plastic matting on the landing slopes coming apart in strips; a visitor in 2025 called it an ecological time bomb.

The jumps cost about €34M. Ski jumping is a tiny sport in Italy, and after the Olympics there were few events to fill them. Summer jumping and "tubing" down the slopes were tried and failed. The Olympic hills don't even belong to the town, which makes any plan harder.

Unlike the bob track at Cesana, they are being kept: it's too expensive to dismantle them. The area at the bottom is being rebuilt for biathlon and roller-skiing (about €5M, aimed at winter 2026–27), so expect building sites below the jumps.
See it from the valley road and the village: the jumps are visible from far away, which is part of the strangeness. The Forte di Fenestrelle is further down the same valley, so you can combine them.
pragelato.s: Local press (2025–26), via the Turin research report

p: Ivrea was Olivetti's company town, and the whole 20th-century part of it is a UNESCO site (since 2018). The star for this map is Talponia, the "mole's house": a crescent of 82 flats about 300 m long cut into a hillside, with a grass roof you can walk on, so from above you see only a lawn and a curved line of glass. In the town centre, Hotel La Serra is a sculptural concrete block of the late 1960s by Cappai and Mainardis.

Adriano Olivetti, who ran the typewriter company from the 1930s to his death in 1960, believed a factory should serve its community: he gave workers libraries, nurseries, housing, health care and good architecture, and hired the best Italian architects to build them. Along Via Jervis you can walk the whole idea: Figini and Pollini's ICO works, which grew from an 1898 red-brick shed into long glass curtain walls; their social-services building opposite (library, welfare, infirmary); Gino Valle's 1980s offices; and the open-air MaAM museum, with seven stations along 2 km.

Talponia came after Adriano's death: the company commissioned it from Gabetti and Isola in 1968 to house visiting staff, and it was finished in 1970. Its excavation, and La Serra's, turned up Roman remains. Nearby, the Sacro Cuore church (designed 1956–58) is all concrete, its thin walls planted in the ground like blades. Olivetti itself declined in the 1980s–90s, so much of what you see is a town built for a company that no longer exists.

Talponia is lived in, so walk past quietly; one flat is a private Olivetti house-museum with its own terms. The UNESCO Visitor Centre at Via Jervis 11 opened in September 2026: free, Tue–Sun 10–18 until 15 November, with weekend guided walks at 10:00 and 15:00 (the Welcome Tours last about 2.5 hours). Ivrea is about an hour by train. It is the best single concrete day trip from Turin.
ivrea.s: UNESCO / Ivrea Visitor Centre; idealista/news (Sep 2026); MiC Censimento

p: On the roof of this long factory, 28 metres above the street, is a banked test track for cars. Fiat built cars in the Lingotto floor by floor going up: raw materials came in at the bottom, and the finished car came out on top and was driven round the roof before going down a spiral ramp. Today the track is a garden of about 40,000 plants, with Renzo Piano's glass "Bubble" meeting room and the Pinacoteca Agnelli's gallery sitting on the roof.

The building went up in 1916–23, designed by Giacomo Mattè Trucco after Fiat's founders had seen Ford's plants in America. It was a concrete manifesto: Le Corbusier put it in *Vers une architecture* as one of the great sights of modern industry. In the film *The Italian Job* (1969) the Minis race across this roof, and that is how most people first saw it. Production ended in 1982, as Mirafiori had long since taken over.

Piano converted the building in the 1980s–90s into a mix of shopping centre, hotels, auditorium, university and offices, keeping the track. Whether that was a rescue or a defeat for an industrial monument is still argued about in Turin.

Go up through the Pinacoteca Agnelli, open Tue–Sun 10–19, closed Monday; last entry 18:30. A new exhibition opens on 30 October 2026 and winter hours can change, so check pinacoteca-agnelli.it. Prices differ by source: the tourist board gives €4 (€2 reduced) for the track alone and €12 (€8) with the gallery; other guides say about €3. It sometimes closes early for private events. It's a tourist sight, but walking the banked curve is worth it.

A brick church with seven 35-metre towers, and next to it an old 60-metre steelworks chimney wrapped in a steel spiral with a cross on top. This is Mario Botta's Church of the Holy Face (2004–06), built on the site of Fiat's steelworks in northern Turin. Behind it, Parco Dora keeps the skeletons of the old factory sheds, steel frames with no walls, and the concrete cooling tanks as a public park.

This whole stretch along the Dora river was the "city of labour": Fiat Ferriere, Michelin and other plants. When they closed in the 1990s, the city redeveloped the land as Spina 3, with housing, the park and the church. Botta, the Swiss architect who also built Évry cathedral near Paris, was asked to keep a memory of the workers, so the chimney became the bell tower. Oddly, the bells actually hang at its base.

It was inaugurated in December 2006, billed as Turin's first church of the 21st century. It also holds the diocese's offices and an underground conference centre. Inside, the light falls from the towers onto a large image of the Holy Face of the Shroud of Turin, which gives the church its name.

The tourist board lists it as open daily 8:00–18:00, with entry limited at busy times. The park is public and always open: walk under the steel frames, the most striking part of the site. The Michelin chimney is in the same park.
santovolto.s: Report on Turin's concrete sites, Oct 2026; Diocese of Turin; Turismo Torino; Infobuild

p: A cemetery that looks like a landscape: about 69 hectares of rolling lawns at the south-west edge of Turin, with the Alps behind. The concrete burial blocks are hidden under artificial hills, and in the open fields the graves are simple slabs set flush in the grass. There are Islamic, Evangelical and Romanian Orthodox sections, with an Orthodox chapel.

It was built in 1969–72, when the old Monumentale cemetery was full. Turin had grown fast: hundreds of thousands of people had moved up from southern Italy to work at Fiat, and the city needed somewhere for them to be buried too. Its designers copied the Nordic "park cemetery" (the Woodland Cemetery in Stockholm is the famous model): no grand family tombs, the same simple slab for everyone, in a park. It has been called egalitarian modernism.

It hasn't been loved. A recent Politecnico thesis calls it an oversized necropolis that history did not favour, and much of it is still empty. Later additions include a "Hill of Memory" garden and plans for a crematorium that has never been built. A memorial to the 64 victims of the Cinema Statuto fire is here too.
Municipal and free; check opening hours on the city website. Compare it with the crematorium garden at the Monumentale, the city's other modern landscape for the dead.
cimiteroparco.s: Comune di Torino; Politecnico di Torino (thesis, 2023); A&RT (2007)

p: Under Piazza Risorgimento lie three parallel concrete galleries, each about 40 metres long and 4.5 metres wide, 12 metres underground, with walls 80 cm thick. Painted on the walls are the original wartime rules: no smoking, stay calm, keep the passages clear. Up in the square, the entrance turrets now carry murals by the street artist XEL, so most people walk past them without guessing what's below.

Turin was one of the most bombed cities in Italy because of its factories: Fiat made aircraft engines and trucks. Raids began on 12 June 1940, two days after Italy entered the war, and lasted until 5 April 1945, killing 2,069 people. The worst were the RAF night raids of November–December 1942. At first most people sheltered in cellars marked with a painted "R"; between 1942 and 1944 the city built about 45 public shelters like this one.
This is one of the best preserved, and it gives you the feeling of the war more directly than any museum: the low ceiling, the benches, the rules on the walls.

It opens only on special days: Museo Diffuso della Resistenza tours, FAI days and Monumenti Aperti. Book through the Museo Diffuso (011 01120780). If you can't get in, the shelter under Le Nuove prison runs regular guided tours.
rifugio.s: Museo Diffuso della Resistenza; Monumenti Aperti

p: Sixteen identical eight-storey slabs lined up in parallel rows on Corso Taranto, 652 flats in heavy prefabricated concrete. The rows are set on the "heliothermic axis", turned so every flat gets the same sun, a rule of modernist planning that produces exactly this regimented look. In spirit, if not in scale, it is Turin's version of Gdańsk's Falowiec or Émile Aillaud's estates around Paris.

It was designed by Nello Renacco in the late 1960s for the families of southern migrants who had come to work at Fiat. Turin then grew by hundreds of thousands of people in two decades, and estates like this went up fast at the city's northern edge, often before schools, shops or buses arrived.

What makes it more than a block of flats is its people. Its tenants' committee is one of the oldest in the city, fighting for repairs, rents and services, and it celebrated 50 years in 2017. The 2020 book *Abitare i margini* tells the story of its housing struggles in the 1970s.
Lived-in social housing: look from the street, and don't photograph people. The Trincerone and Falchera are in the same part of the city.
taranto.s: Abitare i margini (2020). Map pin approximate

p: A church of bare red brick under a roof of exposed concrete folded into a pattern of triangles. The side walls zig-zag in seven segments on each side, set at 60 degrees, and these angled brick fins carry the roof. Inside, the folds and skylights of the concrete ceiling make the light fall unevenly, so the space feels like it is moving.

It was built in 1955–57 for Mirafiori Nord, a new neighbourhood for the families of workers at the nearby Fiat plant. The architects were Nicola Mosso and his son Leonardo, who was then working with Alvar Aalto in Finland. The whole building is planned on a three-dimensional grid of triangles: the roof's beams form equilateral triangles 3 metres deep, and that module sets the position of everything else. *Casabella* published it in 1959.

It became a model: Mosso's own San Pietro in Vincoli at Moriondo and the big church at Nichelino copy its roof idea, and it is considered his most important church. The roof was restored in 2002, and a side chapel was renovated in 2023 with a large painted cross by Giuseppe Cordiano hanging above the altar.
It's an active parish, so go around Mass times to see inside; the outside is plain, and the point is the ceiling.
redentore.s: Casabella 229 (1959), via Atlante IUAV; SOS Brutalism; La Voce e il Tempo (2023–24)

p: A brick-clad office tower on Piazza Statuto, with bay windows jutting out of the façade and arcades at its foot. It was designed by the Milan firm BBPR for the insurer Reale Mutua, and it is Turin's cousin of their famous Torre Velasca in Milan: modern in structure, but deliberately heavy and historical-looking.

BBPR (Banfi, Belgiojoso, Peressutti and Rogers) were the leading Milan architects of the postwar years. In the 1950s they and others reacted against the glass boxes of international modernism by bringing back local materials and historical forms. Critics like Reyner Banham attacked this as a retreat; its defenders said it respected the city. In Turin, a city of brick and arcades, the arcades at the base are the giveaway.
Dates differ between sources: 1955–59 or 1959–61. It's offices, so outside only. The Guglia Beccaria and the Frejus monument are in the same square.

A marble plaque on the building at Via Carlo Alberto 6, facing Piazza Carlo Alberto, marks where Friedrich Nietzsche spent his last lucid months. His room was on the fourth floor, the fifth window from the corner, above what is now the Galleria Subalpina entrance. Stand in the square and look up: the view he had is the one you have, the back of Palazzo Carignano and the hills beyond.

He arrived in April 1888 and fell in love with the city. In letters he praised its arcades, its quiet aristocratic streets, its light and its food, and called it the first place where he felt possible. He came back on 21 September and rented a room from the newsagent Davide Fino for 30 lire a month. In those few months he wrote at an astonishing pace: he finished *Twilight of the Idols* and *The Antichrist*, and wrote *Ecce Homo* and *Nietzsche contra Wagner*, and went to hear Bizet's *Carmen* again and again.

On 3 January 1889 he collapsed in the street. In the days after, he sent friends the "madness letters" signed "Dionysus" and "The Crucified". His friend Franz Overbeck came from Basel and took him away on 9 January; he never recovered and died in 1900. The famous story that he threw his arms round a horse being beaten by its driver and broke down weeping is uncertain: most sources put it in this square, one in Piazza San Carlo, and several call it more legend than fact. It inspired Béla Tarr's film *The Turin Horse* (2011).

The flat is private; the plaque is always visible. You are in the middle of a tight cluster: Palazzo Campana is a few doors down, Palazzo Carignano and Del Cambio are round the corner, and the Galleria Subalpina, which he walked through daily, opens below his window.
nietzsche.s: Report on Turin's thinkers' sites, Oct 2026; Nietzsche's letters (general knowledge)

p: A grand palazzo a few doors from Nietzsche's plaque, now the university's mathematics building. It is the only public building in Turin still named after a partisan, and the name has a story.

Under Fascism it was the Casa del Littorio, seat of the party in Turin; Mussolini spoke from its side balcony. During the occupation the Black Brigades held and interrogated partisans here. On 28 April 1945 partisans of the Giustizia e Libertà brigade "Campana" occupied it, and the building took the name of their commander, Felice Cordero di Pamparato, nom de guerre "Campana", whom the Black Brigades had hanged at Giaveno on 17 August 1944.

On 27 November 1967 students occupied it, an episode usually counted as the start of Italy's 1968 student movement. So in 25 years the building went from the Fascist party to the Resistance to the student revolt.
The courtyard is usually open in term time. Look for plaques inside.
campana.s: MuseoTorino; Istoreto; Wikisource (Cordero di Pamparato); Papuzzi, La Stampa (1997)

p: Black iron cannonballs set into the plaster of Turin's façades, left there on purpose as memorials. The easiest to find are the two on the north wall of the courtyard of Palazzo Saluzzo Paesana (Via della Consolata 1 bis), and several around Piazza San Carlo. Once you have seen one, you start looking up at every old wall.

Most are French shot from the siege of 1706. In the War of the Spanish Succession, Duke Vittorio Amedeo II had switched sides against Louis XIV, and from May to September 1706 a French army besieged Turin and bombarded the city. Underground, miners fought in the tunnels around the citadel; that is where Pietro Micca died. On 7 September 1706 Prince Eugene of Savoy and the Duke broke the siege in a battle north-west of the city. It made the Duke a king a few years later, and he vowed to build the basilica of Superga on the hill from which he had watched the French lines.

Other balls are from 1799, during the wars of the French Revolution. The French held the Cittadella and fired on the city when Suvorov's Austro-Russian army took it. These were walled in too, as a second layer of memory.

A 2025 local guide lists about ten spots: in Piazza San Carlo, on Palazzo Solaro del Borgo, two on the east side near Via Giolitti, and one in the arcade above the Mokika café; inside the MAO; on the façade of the Oratorio di San Filippo Neri in Via Maria Vittoria; on the building north of Via Palazzo di Città on Piazza Palazzo di Città; on the west wall of the Aula di Sant'Andrea at the Consolata; and three at Santa Maria del Monte (Cappuccini). The Palazzo Saluzzo Paesana courtyard is open in business hours.
cannonballs.s: GuidaTorino (2025); Piemonte Italia; general history of the 1706 siege. Map pin approximate

p: A tall, thin, wedge-shaped house on the corner of Corso San Maurizio, whose narrow end is only 54 cm wide. Turin calls it the "Fetta di Polenta", the slice of polenta, for its shape and its yellow colour. From the front it looks like an ordinary building; walk round the corner and it almost disappears.

It was built from 1840 by Alessandro Antonelli, the architect of the Mole Antonelliana, on a leftover triangle of land he owned. Its official name is Casa Scaccabarozzi, after his wife. Nobody believed it would stand, and the story is that Antonelli moved in himself to prove it was safe. It survived the earthquake of 1887 and the wartime bombing.

Antonelli loved pushing structures to their limits: the Mole was meant to be a synagogue and became, for a time, the tallest masonry building in the world. This house is the same idea at domestic scale.
Private building; view it from the street, from both sides, to see the trick.
fetta.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026; general knowledge

p: A tiny café of 31 m² under the arcades of Piazza Castello, all marble, mirrors, bronze and a coffered wooden ceiling. Inside, a plaque says that in 1926 Signora Angela Demichelis Nebiolo invented the tramezzino here, the crustless white-bread triangle sandwich now found in every Italian bar.

The name is credited to Gabriele D'Annunzio. Under Fascism, foreign words were frowned upon, and "tramezzino" (a little "in-between") replaced the English "sandwich". Sources give 1925 or 1926 for the invention. The café has been a listed historic shop since 1985.

Turin is full of such "firsts" (vermouth, gianduiotto, grissini, bicerin), some well documented and some marketing. This one at least has a plaque and a date, and you can still eat the thing at the counter where it started.
Open roughly 09:30–20:00 (19:30 on Tue and Wed). Have a tramezzino; that is the point.

Guarino Guarini's Baroque palace (1679) with its rippling brick façade, one of the great buildings of Turin. Two kings were born here, Carlo Alberto and Vittorio Emanuele II, the first king of Italy. Behind the façade is the chamber of the Subalpine Parliament of the Kingdom of Sardinia, and it was here, in 1861, that the first Italian Parliament proclaimed the Kingdom of Italy.

The new parliament outgrew the old chamber, so a much bigger hall and a new wing were built on the back of the palace, facing Piazza Carlo Alberto. By the time it was finished, in 1864–65, the capital had moved to Florence, and the great chamber was never used. That is the story behind the riots of 1864 (see the bullet dent in Piazza San Carlo).

Today the palace holds the Museo Nazionale del Risorgimento, where you can see both chambers. It is a famous sight, so lower priority, but it anchors a tight cluster: Del Cambio is opposite, and Nietzsche's plaque and Palazzo Campana are a minute away.

The museum is open Tue–Sun 10:00–18:00 (last entry 17:00), closed Monday; about €10 (€8 reduced), free with the Abbonamento Musei; check current prices. Look at the façade from Piazza Carignano, then walk round to see the later one on Piazza Carlo Alberto.
carignano.s: General history; check museum site; Museo Nazionale del Risorgimento

p: A small plaque in Piazza San Carlo for the victims of the night of 3 June 2017. Tens of thousands of people were watching the Juventus Champions League final against Real Madrid on a big screen when a gang of young robbers sprayed pepper spray to cause panic and steal in the confusion. The crowd stampeded.

Three people eventually died and around 1,600 were hurt, many cut by broken glass. Members of the gang were convicted, and four people, including organisers, were convicted of manslaughter for the safety failures. Since then, big public screenings in Italian squares have had much stricter rules.
The plaque was placed in 2019. Pin approximate: look along the square's edges.
sancarlo.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026; general news coverage. Map pin approximate

p: Look up at the fourth-floor corner of Piazzetta Corpus Domini 19: an oversized metal ring pierces the corner of an 18th-century building, like an earring. It is *Baci Urbani*, "urban kisses", an art installation meant to be temporary that was simply never taken down.

It's a small joke on an old building, and a good example of Turin's habit of contemporary art in its historic streets (the upside-down David and the bull bursting from a wall are others on this map). Most people walk underneath without noticing it.
The little square around it, with the church of Corpus Domini, is where a legendary miracle of the host is said to have happened in 1453.
baci.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026

p: A restaurant open since 1757, with red velvet, mirrors and gilded stucco, facing Palazzo Carignano across the square. In the main room, the table where Count Cavour used to sit is still kept and marked with a small plaque. From it he could watch the doors of the parliament opposite, and the story is that his staff would come and fetch him when a vote was near.

Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour, was prime minister of Piedmont and then the first prime minister of Italy, the diplomat who more than anyone made unification happen. Palazzo Carignano held the Subalpine Parliament and, in 1861, the first Italian Parliament, which proclaimed the Kingdom of Italy. So this dining room is where much of that politics was talked over. Cavour died in June 1861, three months after the proclamation, at his house a few streets away.

The table is well documented: both the regional tourism site and *Rolling Stone Italia* confirm it. The longer lists of famous guests (Casanova, Puccini, Balzac, Nietzsche, Verdi) are promotional and unverified.

It has a Michelin star and is expensive. Dinner runs roughly 19:30–23:30, with Sunday lunch, and there is a cheaper bistro at lunch. You can ask for Cavour's table when you book (delcambio.it). Of all the "sit where they sat" places in Turin, this is the most honest.
cambio.s: Piemonte Italia; Rolling Stone Italia; delcambio.it

p: A café under the arcades of Piazza Vittorio Veneto, with its original red marble tables, wooden counter and old mirrors. Cesare Pavese spent his time writing here, and the city itself says that you can have breakfast where he wrote. It is the best documented of the cafés linked to him.

Pavese was Turin's great 20th-century writer: novelist, poet, translator of American literature (Melville, Faulkner, Steinbeck) and an editor at the publisher Einaudi. Confined by the Fascists in 1935, he wrote about loneliness and the hills of Piedmont, and his diary *The Business of Living* is one of the great Italian books of the century. He won the Strega Prize in June 1950 and killed himself two months later in a hotel room near Porta Nuova (that hotel is also on this map).

Piazza Vittorio is one of the largest arcaded squares in Europe, opening at its end onto the Po and the church of the Gran Madre. The café is also linked to vermouth: Giuseppe Carpano is said to have refined his recipe here around 1889–1902, so a vermouth is the fitting order. A blog says Nietzsche "certainly" came here; there is no evidence for it.
Open Mon–Fri 08–00 (closed Wednesday), Sat 09–01, Sun 09–00. Sit inside, at a marble table, and take your time.

A café on Via Po open since 1780, with velvet sofas, mirrors and gilded rooms behind the arcade. It was the café of the Piedmontese establishment in the 19th century, and it is famous for its ice cream.

Rattazzi, D'Azeglio, Balbo, Santorre di Santarosa and Cavour came here; Cavour is said to have founded his Whist Club in its rooms. Its regulars were conservative aristocrats and officials, so Turin nicknamed it the café of the "Machiavellis and pigtails" (pigtails, codini, meant reactionaries who still wore their hair in the old style). King Carlo Alberto supposedly asked each morning, "What are they saying at Fiorio?", to take the pulse of the court. The patriots met at San Carlo instead.
Nietzsche is linked to it through its ice cream; plausible, but only popular sources say so.
It's at Via Po 8; one guide gives a wrong address on Piazza Castello. Check hours. Have a gelato under the arcades of Via Po, one of the longest arcaded streets in Europe.

A tiny café of 1763 facing the Consolata sanctuary, with a handful of marble tables, wooden panelling and candlelight. The bicerin was born here: espresso, hot chocolate and cream, layered in a small glass and not stirred.

It was a drink for people coming out of Mass at the Consolata, Turin's favourite church, after fasting: hot, sweet and filling. By long tradition Cavour drank here while waiting for the royal family to leave the sanctuary. The café has been run by women for most of its history, which was unusual.

The famous names on the walls (Dumas, Puccini, Nietzsche, Gozzano, Calvino) are tradition, and even the Cavour story is usually told as "legend has it". The firmest literary link is fictional: Umberto Eco set a scene of *The Prague Cemetery* here.
Closed Wednesdays; roughly 08:30–19:30. It's tiny, so expect a queue. The Consolata has cannonballs in one wall, and the Farmacia della Consolata is nearby.

A grand café of 1822 under the arcades of Piazza San Carlo, with chandeliers, mirrors and gilded stucco. It was the meeting place of Risorgimento patriots, D'Azeglio, Cavour, Rattazzi, Giolitti and Crispi, and the police closed it several times on suspicion of subversion.

It claims to have been the first café in Italy lit by gas. A literary circle met here in the 1920s. In 1899 the Duke of the Abruzzi is said to have planned his polar expedition here (sources say "Antarctic", but his voyage went to the Arctic).
The line that Gramsci conceived *L'Ordine Nuovo* here is a stock marketing phrase with no scholarly source. It's a good example of how Turin's historic cafés sell their past.
Open roughly 08:00–00:00. It was closed for restoration in 1953–63, and the management has changed several times. The bullet dent and the brass bull are in the same square.

An 1870s café on Corso Vittorio Emanuele II with a gilded, mirrored interior, one of Turin's classic historic cafés. Popular sources list Luigi Einaudi (economist and later President of Italy), Cesare Pavese, Natalia Ginzburg and the founders of Fiat and Lavazza among its regulars.

Turin's café culture grew with the city's role as a capital: officials, writers, officers and businessmen needed somewhere to meet, and the cafés became semi-public offices. Platti served the new bourgeois district around Porta Nuova.

It has had a bumpy history: it went bankrupt and closed in 2015 before reopening, and changed owners again at the end of September 2026. The new owners restored the original counter, mirrors and frescoes, renewed the upstairs rooms and reopened on 23 October 2026, with café and pastry downstairs and a restaurant upstairs. Worth a look to see how they treated the old rooms.
platti.s: ANSA (Oct 2026); Caffè Platti; Quotidiano Piemontese (23 Oct 2026)

p: The Royal Library: a long hall with a painted barrel vault, wooden shelves on two levels and a gallery, designed by Pelagio Palagi in the 1830s, under the palace's main wing on Piazza Castello. It feels like a library that has been in use for two centuries, because it has.

King Carlo Alberto founded it in 1831–37 to gather the Savoy family's books, manuscripts and drawings. Its treasures include drawings by Leonardo da Vinci bought in 1840, among them the red-chalk drawing traditionally called his self-portrait and his Codex on the Flight of Birds. These are kept in a vault and shown only in special exhibitions, but they are the reason scholars come.

I found no sourced list of famous readers, so this isn't a "sat where X sat" stop; it's a "sit in a great reading room" one. Until 6 January 2027 the hall also hosts an exhibition on Queen Margherita, Italy's first queen.

Tourists see the hall with a Musei Reali ticket: Mon and Fri 9:00–13:30; Tue, Thu and Sat 13:30–18:30. The reading room is for adult researchers only, booked by email at least 24 hours ahead (Mon and Fri 13:30–18:30; Tue, Thu and Sat 8:30–13:30; closed Wednesday).

Turin's Academy of Sciences sits in Guarini's Collegio dei Nobili, the same Baroque building that houses the Egyptian Museum. Its library, founded in 1783, keeps two great Coronelli globes, a celestial and a terrestrial one, and two centuries of scientific books.

The Academy grew out of a private society founded in 1757 by the young Joseph-Louis Lagrange and two friends; it became royal in 1783. Its early members included Monge, Laplace, d'Alembert and Euler. Turin's first proper observatory, the Specola, was built on its top floor in 1789–90 by Francesco Feroggio. After more than 80 years unused, it reopened in January 2026 as a multimedia production space run with the Politecnico.
Lagrange was born a few streets away (his plaque is on this map) and became one of the greatest mathematicians of all time; in Paris he chaired the commission that created the metric system.
Visits are by appointment only (Mon–Thu 9–13 and 15–17, Fri 9–13, through a form). Casual visitors usually get in only during events and talks.
accademia.s: Accademia delle Scienze di Torino; general history; Schiavone, Torino Storia (2020); Politecnico di Torino (Jan 2026)

p: From Piazza Castello you see only the old 18th-century façade. Behind it Carlo Mollino built an entirely new opera house: a curving brick and concrete shell, a foyer with walkways in the air under a ceiling of exposed concrete shapes, and an auditorium shaped like a half-open oyster, with 1,398 red seats in the stalls. Over it hangs Mollino's "chandelier", not glass drops but 1,762 thin aluminium stems with lights and 1,900 reflective perspex rods, like stalactites in a cave.

The first Teatro Regio opened in 1740, by Benedetto Alfieri, and was one of the grandest opera houses in Europe, with 2,500 seats. On the night of 8–9 February 1936 a fire started under the stage and destroyed everything but the façade. A competition was held, but war and money got in the way, and the site stayed a ruin for 30 years. Mollino and the engineer Marcello Zavelani Rossi got the job in 1965; work began in 1967 and it reopened on 10 April 1973 with Verdi's *I vespri siciliani*, staged by Maria Callas.

Mollino was Turin's great eccentric: architect, furniture designer, racing driver, pilot, skier and secret photographer. He designed every detail here, from the door handles to the lamps, and his signature is the curved line, a modern echo of the Baroque. He died in August 1973, months after the opening, so this is his last major work and his largest. The Piccolo Regio below seats 380.

The backstage tours ("Il Regio dietro le quinte") last an hour: Sat 15:00 and 16:30, Sun 11:00, except holidays and show days. €10 (€5 under 18), Italian only, max 25 people. Tickets go online from the Monday before each month's first tour, so book early. Better still, see an opera. The Palazzo degli Affari and the Lago Nero sled station make a Mollino thread across the map.
regio.s: Teatro Regio; en.wikipedia; Italia.it; divisare; Atti e Rassegna Tecnica (1973)

p: The Chamber of Commerce by Carlo Mollino and partners (1964–73): a block raised on a single central core so it seems to hover over the street, a four-storey "blade" linked to it by a walkway in the air, and inside, Mollino's spiral staircase.

Mollino and his team won a 1964 competition against 29 others, on the site of a palace destroyed by bombs. During building the central pylon and the gap above the base were made smaller, which hides some of the original daring. It was finished the same year as his Teatro Regio, so 1973 was Mollino's year.

It's working public offices, so you can usually step in during opening hours to see the stair. The architecture foundation has run occasional paid tours (€6). The Ex Borsa is next door, and the two make a fine pair of 1950s–70s Turin.
affari.s: Camera di commercio Torino; TorinoToday; MiC Censimento

p: The old stock exchange: a trading hall under a vaulted concrete roof with a distinctive pattern of ribs, facing Piazzale Valdo Fusi. It was won in competition in 1953 by Roberto Gabetti, Aimaro Isola and the engineer Giuseppe Raineri, and built in 1952–56.

It's an early work of Gabetti and Isola, the Turin pair who later built Talponia at Ivrea and the factory-shed church at Piossasco. Here they were young and still experimenting, part of the Neoliberty generation that wanted modern architecture to be warmer and more crafted.

Trading ended in 1992, when Italy moved all trading to Milan and to screens, and it has been shut ever since.
