A €14.6M conversion by Isolarchitetti (the firm's successors) is planned as part of an "Innovation Block" with the Chamber of Commerce next door, but works may not start until 2028, with completion around 2030.
Outside only, from the square.
borsa.s: MuseoTorino; Torino Oggi (Sep 2026). Map pin approximate

p: The university's humanities building of the late 1960s–1970 on Via Sant'Ottavio: a huge slab on an exposed steel frame, one of the first of its kind in Turin. Steel, not concrete, but brutal in mass. Students call it simply "Palazzo Nuovo", the new building.

It has been criticised since it went up for pushing a giant into the historic centre. It was built for the boom of student numbers in the 1960s and opened as the 1968 movement was starting, so it became the stage of Turin's student politics: assemblies, occupations, posters. It still is: it was occupied and shut for a week in early 2026. Felice Bardelli, one of its designers, also built the Gesù Operaio church.
In the 2010s asbestos was found and the building was closed for a long cleanup; later steel stair inserts changed its look.
It's open in university hours; walk the ground floor to feel the scale.

A block of flats in Borgo Crimea whose façades ripple like fabric: horizontal bands of cast "litocemento" running across undulating walls, deep balconies, and an entrance shaped like an oyster shell with concave steps. It's named after the obelisk in the square in front. Inside, no two floor plans are the same.

Sergio Jaretti and Elio Luzi built it in 1954–59, and it became the icon of Turin's "Neoliberty", a movement of young Turin and Milan architects who rejected the plain boxes of international modernism and looked back to Art Nouveau (called Liberty in Italy), to Gaudí and to Frank Lloyd Wright. In 1959 the critic Reyner Banham attacked them in an article called "Neoliberty: the Italian retreat from modern architecture", and the debate made them famous.

Turin was the movement's home: Gabetti and Isola's Bottega d'Erasmo and their Ex Borsa are from the same moment, and Jaretti and Luzi went on to build the Torri Pitagora. Seen today, the Casa dell'Obelisco looks less like a retreat than like an early sign of the postmodern taste that came 20 years later.
Private flats: look from Piazza Crimea, at the foot of the hill across the Po.

Two ten-storey towers on Corso Siracusa that stand on a forest of thick pillars and grow heavier as they rise, with deep balconies stacked on top of each other. They look as if they were built upside down, which is exactly the point.

Jaretti and Luzi designed them in 1962–68. The 1959 zoning rules limited how much floor area a building could have at different heights, and the architects worked out a "desirability diagram" that showed where flats were worth most: higher up, with views and light. So they took space away from the ground floor and put it at the top. The pillared base also leaves an open, shaded space at street level.

They belong to the same experimental Turin as the Casa dell'Obelisco, by the same architects. Other Jaretti and Luzi housing to drive past: Corso Orbassano 268, Via Curtatone 3, Via Breglio/Via Bibiana, Piazza Rebaudengo (1966) and Piazza Statuto (1958–59).
Private, outside only; Open House Torino has sometimes opened them. Stand under the pillars and look up.
pitagora.s: MuseoTorino; MiC Censimento; Open House Italia

p: At the northern edge of Turin, a village of three-storey red-brick blocks laid out on a hexagonal grid, grouped in three- and four-armed clusters around green courts and a small civic centre with a concrete mushroom column. It feels more like a planned garden town than an estate. This is Falchera, the city's first postwar housing satellite.

It was built in 1951–60 under INA-Casa, the national plan launched in 1949 to house workers and create jobs after the war. The planner, Giovanni Astengo, was close to Adriano Olivetti's "Comunità" movement, which wanted neighbourhoods built at a human scale around schools, churches and shops, like Italian villages. Falchera was meant as a manifesto of that "organic neighbourhood".

Just north, Falchera Nuova (early 1970s) shows what came next: sixteen 10-storey prefab towers built fast for the wave of migrants coming to Fiat. Walking from one to the other is a short lesson in how Italian housing changed in twenty years.
Public streets. The architecture foundation runs guided walks, meeting at Viale Falchera 80. San Michele Arcangelo church is a short walk away.
falchera.s: MiC Censimento; Archivi degli Architetti (SAN); Fondazione per l'architettura

p: Seventy-one hectares of public housing at the north-west edge of Turin, built in 1958–68 by 45 architects working in nine teams, including Gabetti and Isola, Levi Montalcini and Cavallari Murat. Brick towers, slabs and Scandinavian-style courtyards sit side by side, so the estate reads like an anthology of 1960s Turin housing.

It was planned for 20,000 people under the national public housing programme, as Fiat's workforce grew. It was far from the centre, poorly served, and quickly got a bad reputation; Turin's new prison, built here in the 1980s to replace Le Nuove, made "Vallette" synonymous with jail.
Architecturally, though, it is the richest estate in the city. Gabetti and Isola's middle school at Via dei Mughetti 26 breaks the usual school block into pieces.
Public streets. The local history centre gives tours during Open House.
vallette.s: MuseoTorino; Open House Torino; MiC Censimento. Map pin approximate

p: An all-concrete church in Madonna di Campagna: a central plan under a complicated roof that rests on massive pillars and seems to float above a continuous ribbon of windows. From inside, the walls don't seem to reach the ceiling, so the roof hangs over you in light.

It was built in 1967–69 by the engineer Mario Bianco, during the boom of church building in Turin's outskirts after the Second Vatican Council. Cardinal Michele Pellegrino, archbishop from 1965 to 1977 and known as the "workers' cardinal", wanted modest, modern churches close to the new working-class estates, open to the neighbourhood rather than monumental. The diocese counts 116 such churches.
Most were cheap and plain; this one is among the boldest. Bianco also designed San Francesco di Sales.
Active parish; go around Mass times to see the roof from inside.
sanpaoloap.s: MuseoTorino; Diocese of Turin (Zito, Casa tra le case)

p: A post-Council church whose tall bell tower and sloping roof dominate the low skyline of its neighbourhood. In 2010 Turin's order of architects named it one of the most mature church designs of the period.

It belongs to the wave of new parishes built for the outskirts in the 1960s–70s, after the Second Vatican Council had asked for churches that gathered the community around the altar. The dates differ: 1961 or 1970 (probably the full complex). The liturgical area was altered in 2013.
Active parish; go around Mass times to see inside.
santateresa.s: OAT; CEI Chiese italiane. Map pin approximate

p: A 1963–67 church in Barriera di Milano dedicated to "Jesus the Worker", in one of Turin's most working-class districts. It's by the engineer Felice Bardelli, who also co-designed Palazzo Nuovo; the national church census singles out its structural system. Under the church there's a basketball and volleyball gym.

The gym says a lot: these new parishes were meant to be centres of neighbourhood life for migrant families who had little else, with sport, youth clubs and meeting rooms. Cardinal Pellegrino consecrated it in 1967.
Exposed concrete is not confirmed, so check in person before giving it time.
A 1967–71 church by Mario Federico Roggero, built in the middle of the Mirafiori Sud public housing estates, in the shadow of the Fiat plant. It's also a venue for the MITO music festival.

Mirafiori Sud was built in the 1960s–70s almost entirely for Fiat workers' families, and the church was one of the few public buildings when it opened. Roggero designed several of Turin's post-Council churches.
Exposed concrete unconfirmed. Go at Mass times (Sat 18:15, Sun 9:30, 11:00, 18:15) to see inside. Pair it with the Mirafiori factory front.
sanluca.s: MuseoTorino; Diocese of Turin. Map pin approximate

p: A 1967–70 church by Enzo Dolci and Antonino Tripodi, with a pointed, spire-like roof, at the edge of Falchera. The national church census flags its structure as notable.
It served the new estates of Falchera and Pietra Alta. Materials are unconfirmed: a pass-by to check in person, a short walk from Astengo's village.
A 1973–78 church in the San Paolo district by the engineer Mario Bianco, the designer of San Paolo Apostolo, Turin's boldest all-concrete church. That family link is the reason it's on the map.

San Paolo was one of Turin's historic working-class "borghi", home to the Lancia works and to strikes and Resistance fighters. The church was one of the last of the post-Council building wave. Its materials are unverified, so treat it as one to check in person.
sanfrancescosales.s: Diocese of Turin catalogue. Map pin approximate

p: A modest 1960s church in Parella by Pasquale Carbonara and Michele Berardo, consecrated in 1966. Even the parish's own blessing text called it small. It replaced a 320 m² chapel that had served the growing district.
It's a fair example of the ordinary post-Council parish: built fast and cheaply for a new neighbourhood, more meeting hall than monument. Only worth it if you pass by.
mariagoretti.s: Parish of Santa Maria Goretti. Map pin approximate

p: In the park by the Italia '61 lake, a concrete viaduct on piers shaped like upside-down pyramids curves over the water and stops in mid-air. These are 14 surviving spans of a 1961 monorail, with the shell of its south station. Their reflection in the lake makes them look even more like a sculpture.

It was built for Italia '61, the exhibition for the centenary of unification, using the Swedish-German Alweg system that had just been demonstrated in Germany and at Disneyland. It opened on 6 May 1961 and ran 1.8 km along the river from a north station near the car museum to this south station by the Palazzo del Lavoro. Visitors loved it, but after the exhibition there was nowhere useful for it to go, and it closed in November 1963. The train burned in its depot in 1979.

Most of the viaduct came down in 1994 after concrete started falling. Some dismantled beams still lie in a field beside the ring road at Nichelino, and others were reported at Collegno; neither is confirmed in 2026. Proposals for a High Line-style walkway have never been funded.

Freely visible in the public park. Expect graffiti, crumbling concrete and some rough sleepers. The abandoned 1961 fountain is nearby, and the Palazzo del Lavoro is at the south end. This is the best place to feel how optimistic 1961 was.
monorail.s: MuseoTorino; TorinoStoria; Amici di Italia '61; artwort. Map pin approximate

p: Near the Palavela, in the Italia '61 park, lie the remains of the illuminated fountain of the 1961 exhibition, when the whole district was lit up at night for the crowds. The Italia '61 volunteer group describes it as still there, though left to itself.

Italia '61 turned this stretch of riverbank into a showcase of modern Italy: the Palazzo del Lavoro, the Palavela, the monorail, pavilions for each region, and fountains and lights. Most of it was temporary; what's left is scattered through the park like the pieces of a puzzle.
Don't confuse it with the fountain at the Valentino entrance. Not re-checked in 2026; it sits next to the monorail stumps.
fontana61.s: Amici di Italia '61. Map pin approximate

p: The monorail's north station of 1961 still stands on Corso Unità d'Italia, now Casa UGI, a home where families of children being treated for cancer can stay near the hospital. The building that once welcomed exhibition crowds now does something quieter and more useful.

The monorail ran from here 1.8 km south to the Palazzo del Lavoro, from May 1961 to November 1963. After it closed the train was stored in the depot here, and on 17 December 1979 it burned and was later scrapped. The only surviving piece is a small metal plate owned by a collector.
It's in use, so look from outside and be discreet. The monorail stumps are further south along the river.

A 69-metre red steel arch rising over the railway yards south of the Lingotto, holding up a footbridge about 400 metres long. Built in 2003–05, it's the most visible legacy of the 2006 Winter Olympics, linking the Lingotto to the former market where the athletes lived.

The athletes' village reused the Mercati Generali, the city's 1932–33 wholesale market by Umberto Cuzzi, with its long arcades, plus new coloured prefab blocks. After the games the village was meant to become housing, but much of it stood empty. From 2013 some of the buildings (the ex-MOI) were occupied by hundreds of refugees and migrants, until they were cleared in 2019. It became a symbol of what happens after the Olympics leave.
The footbridge is public: cross it for the view of the tracks. Some ex-MOI buildings are still empty or fenced.

A railway cutting about 5.5 km long, sunk below street level through northern Turin, abandoned, overgrown with trees and full of dumped rubbish. From the bridges and the street edges you look down into a hidden green valley through the middle of the city.

It was a freight line that linked the railway to the Vanchiglia goods yard and the factories of the north. When the factories closed and the yard went, it was simply left. For years it was one of Turin's urban wildernesses, a place for wildlife, graffiti and illegal dumping.

Not for long. Metro Line 2 will run largely along it: the €1bn tender was published in May 2026, and works on the first section are due to start in the first half of 2027. The plan is three stations and a tree-lined boulevard of 67,000 m². Residents held a sit-in in October 2026.
See it this winter, from public streets only (Via Sempione, Via Gottardo, Corso Regio Parco). In a few years it will be a building site and then a boulevard.

The ruins of OSI-Ghia, a car-body plant built around 1960 and abandoned since 2001. Ghia was one of Turin's famous coachbuilders, the design houses that dressed other companies' cars; OSI was its industrial arm.

Turin was the world capital of car design in the 1950s–60s, with Ghia, Pininfarina, Bertone and Italdesign all here. This plant is a ruin of that world. It's fenced, and local press advises avoiding the area. Exterior only, and only if you are passing.
osighia.s: Torino Cronaca; general history. Map pin approximate

p: Along Corso Regina Margherita stand the huge empty sheds of the ThyssenKrupp steelworks. In the night of 5–6 December 2007, a fire on finishing line 5 engulfed a team of workers; seven of them died, one that night and six in the following weeks.

The plant was already being run down before closure, and the investigation found that safety equipment had been neglected. The company's CEO was at first convicted of murder with "eventual intent", the first such verdict for a workplace death in Italy; on appeal it became manslaughter. Turin took it as a national scandal about workplace safety, and a local paper still calls it an open wound for the city.
This whole western belt was steel country, and the Fiat steelworks next door became Parco Dora.
Fenced, exterior only. Visit with respect.
thyssen.s: L'Unica; general news coverage. Map pin approximate

p: The surviving sheds of the factory where Superga's canvas sneakers were made, abandoned since 1998. The brand, founded in Turin in 1911 and named after the hill, made the white rubber-soled tennis shoe that half of Italy wore.

Production moved away like most of Turin's manufacturing. In July 2026 the city announced a deal to turn the site into a culture hub run by Paratissima, the art fair organisers (€3.5M, about three years of works).
Until then, outside only.
superga_f.s: Torino Cronaca; Torino Oggi (Jul 2026). Map pin approximate

p: The Officine Grandi Motori, Fiat's huge works for marine and industrial engines: about 70,000 m² in Barriera di Milano, emptied gradually from 1971. What's left are dramatic shells seen around a fenced demolition site: the 1911 "Basilica", a nave-like hall, and the "Lingottino" on Corso Vercelli.

Grandi Motori made the diesel engines for ships and submarines; in April 1945 its workers rose against the Germans, and some of its plaques are now in the Cascina Marchesa garden and the Museo Diffuso.

Demolition started in February 2025 and has been slowed by stability checks. The Basilica will become shops, the Lingottino student housing, with a garden and an Esselunga logistics hub. The view changes month by month, so go soon.
ogm.s: ANSA (Feb 2025); Torino Oggi (Jan 2026). Map pin approximate

p: A guided tour that takes you through the cell blocks of Le Nuove, Turin's 19th-century prison, and then 18 metres down into its air-raid shelter. The shelter is concrete, cramped and damp, and the story is told through the testimony of the people who were held above it: political prisoners, partisans and Jews waiting to be deported.

Le Nuove was built in the 1860s–70s as a model prison, with long wings radiating from a centre so that guards could watch every corridor. It was used until 2003. During the German occupation (1943–45) one wing was run by the SS, and many partisans spent their last nights here before being taken to the Martinetto or Pian del Lot to be shot; Jews arrested in Piedmont passed through on their way to Auschwitz. The shelter was for staff and prisoners during the bombing of the city.

Volunteers turned the old prison into a museum, and the tour is unusually moving: you stand in cells where the names of prisoners are still scratched on the walls. Of Turin's shelters, this is the best one to actually visit, with real depth and concrete and a whole history above it.
Guided only, booking required (011 7604881, infoprenotazioni@museolenuove.it). Groups of 25, about 1 h 15. €8 (€5 reduced), free with the Abbonamento Musei.
nuoverifugio.s: Museo del Carcere Le Nuove; Istoreto

p: Ten metres under the Cortile d'Onore of the town hall lies a shelter built in 1940 for city staff: a single room 20 by 3 metres for 50 people, with its original gas-tight doors and the signs painted on the walls.

It was built in the first months of the war, when everyone feared gas attacks as in 1915–18, hence the heavy airtight doors. It's a small, intact time capsule compared with the big public shelters like Piazza Risorgimento.
Free visits have been offered since 2017, with guided visits for groups on the fourth Tuesday of the month booked through the Cerimoniale office. I could not find the current schedule.

visitazione.t: Mirafiori shelter and Chiesa della Visitazione
p: A guided tour in old Mirafiori: it starts at the site of a vanished Savoy castle, visits the Chiesa della Visitazione, a 1934 concrete church with a crypt, and ends in the shelter that protected the village during the war.
Before Fiat, Mirafiori was a village around a ducal country palace; the castle disappeared, and the factory took its name. The tour connects the three Mirafioris: royal, village and industrial.
Run by Arte e Musei, about 90 minutes. No dates were bookable in October 2026, so watch arteemusei.com. Not wheelchair-accessible.
visitazione.s: Arte e Musei. Map pin approximate

p: A concrete sports arena in Parco Ruffini: a big concrete hall in the trees, all structure and roof. It was built in 1959–61 by Annibale Vitellozzi for Italia '61, with Fiat's design office.

Vitellozzi had just designed the Palazzetto dello Sport in Rome with Pier Luigi Nervi for the 1960 Olympics, and this is its Turin twin. He later said that, of all the sports halls he designed, he preferred this one for the daring of its composition. Italia '61 left Turin a whole set of such buildings: the Palazzo del Lavoro, the Palavela and this.

Unlike the Palazzo del Lavoro, it never stopped being used. It was renovated in 2004, seats about 4,000 and is home to the city's basketball team; since 2019 it is officially the Palazzetto dello Sport Gianni Asti.
The outside is free to see in the park. To go in, go to a match or event; watching basketball under Vitellozzi's roof is the best way to see it.

mirafiori.t: Fiat Mirafiori: Palazzina and Corso Tazzoli
p: The Fiat Mirafiori plant: along Corso Agnelli a 220-metre office block clad in white stone, the Palazzina (1937–39), and behind it a brick factory front almost a kilometre long on Corso Tazzoli. The site covers about two square kilometres, a city of its own. Only part of it still makes cars.

Mussolini inaugurated it on 15 May 1939; the story goes that the workers gave him a cold reception. After the war it became the heart of the Italian economic miracle: at its peak in the late 1960s and 70s tens of thousands worked here, many of them migrants from the south who arrived at Porta Nuova with cardboard suitcases. Mirafiori is why Turin doubled in size, why the estates at Falchera and Vallette were built, and why the Cimitero Parco was needed.

It was also the heart of Italian labour history. The great strikes of March 1943, the first mass strikes against Fascism, started inside, in Officina 19. On 3 July 1969 a strike turned into a riot on Corso Traiano by Gate 2, the opening of the "hot autumn". Porta 5 was the gate of the struggles of the 1970s, and the 35-day strike of 1980 ended with the "march of the 40,000" (see Teatro Nuovo). None of these spots has a plaque.
Stellantis plans to reopen the Palazzina as an office campus by 2027, so expect scaffolding. Private: look from the pavement. San Luca Evangelista, in the estates nearby, completes the picture.

socrem.t: Tempio Crematorio and Luogo del Ricordo
p: At the Monumentale cemetery, Turin's crematorium of 1882, the second in Italy after Milan, with a modern garden of grassy slopes and symbolic sculptures by Riccardo Cordero. Next door is the city's Luogo del Ricordo: three fountains over rock gardens of Luserna stone, where ashes are scattered and carried into the ground by the water.

Cremation was a cause of free-thinkers and Freemasons in 19th-century Italy; the Catholic Church banned it until 1963. The SOCREM societies built crematoria to make it possible, and Turin's was one of the first.
Together with the Cimitero Parco, it's the city's other modern landscape for the dead. Open in cemetery hours, free.

Turin's courthouse on Corso Vittorio Emanuele II: a 300-metre building of brick and about 30,000 m² of mirrored glass, seven storeys above ground and three below, built in 1990–2000. It's named after Bruno Caccia, Turin's chief prosecutor, murdered by the 'Ndrangheta in 1983.
It's megastructure scale, but not concrete brutalism, and the architects are disputed. A pass-by only.

A church built from the parts of a factory shed: 24-metre concrete trusses, walls of translucent U-shaped industrial glass, and a single roof 24 by 84 metres covering church, rectory and portico. On the forecourt stands a giant precast concrete cross. It looks like a warehouse until you go inside and see the light coming through the glass.

Gabetti and Isola (with Luciano Re) built it in 1969–73 for the families of workers at Fiat's new plant at Rivalta, many of them recent migrants. They chose catalogue factory components on purpose, both because they were cheap and because they belonged to the workers' world. They called it a church "at the limit of poverty". It has been described as one of the best-known Italian churches of the 1970s.

It is a pure example of the church thinking of the Second Vatican Council, as pushed in Turin by Cardinal Pellegrino: no monument, just a shelter for a community. In 1986–87 the trusses were painted with figures of the apostles, which the national census calls ill-advised. Look up and decide for yourself.
Active parish; open around Mass times. Pair it with Collegno on the same side of the city.

A pentagonal church at Moriondo, near Moncalieri, where six exposed concrete pillars carry a roof broken into triangles, and the light comes in through the gaps between them. It's by Nicola Mosso, a direct sibling of his Redentore in Mirafiori; the national census rates it a work of excellence.
Mosso spent his career on one idea: a roof built from triangles that spreads its load and lets light through the joints. Here he made the whole plan follow it.
Mid-1960s, exact years unconfirmed; the concrete is partly clad in brick. Active parish.

Nichelino's big new church of 1970–73: three aisles under exposed concrete beams that cross upwards into a net, modelled on Mosso's Redentore. It has a concrete frame, exposed brick and large windows, and seats over 600.
Nichelino grew from a village into a dormitory town for Fiat workers in the 1960s, and the old parish church was far too small; this "Chiesa Grande" was the answer.
The parish reports roof leaks and decaying concrete. The building faces Piazza della Libertà (parish address Via Stupinigi 16); check the pin on satellite view.
nichelino.s: Diocese of Turin; nichelino.com. Map pin approximate

p: Oscar Niemeyer in Turin. The FATA headquarters at Pianezza is an office block over 100 metres long that hangs from great arches, so it reads like a bridge on dry land. It rests on just six hollow piers; the side cantilevers reach 21.30 metres, the spans between piers 32.40 metres, and the middle floors are suspended from the arches on steel ties.

Niemeyer, the architect of Brasília and a communist, went into exile in Europe after the 1964 military coup in Brazil and worked for years from Paris. In Italy his best-known work is the Mondadori headquarters near Milan; this is its Turin sibling, designed in 1976–79 with Riccardo Morandi, the engineer of many Italian bridges, as the structural designer. FATA is an engineering firm that builds automated plants.

The national census of postwar architecture describes its "astonishing effect of suspension". It is almost unknown even in Turin. If you saw Niemeyer's buildings in Paris, the Communist Party headquarters and the Bobigny labour exchange, this is the same hand applied to an office building.
It is still FATA's offices at Via dei Prati 2: photograph it from the road and car-park edge, don't enter the grounds. This is the most important new pin on the Turin map.

A Baroque charterhouse with a gateway by Juvarra, and behind it a park of about 40 hectares dotted with long 19th-century pavilions, some restored and some abandoned. For more than a century this was Turin's Royal Asylum, and the park you walk in was enclosed by walls.

The Certosa was founded in the 17th century as a Carthusian monastery under royal patronage. In 1852 it became the Regio Manicomio, the asylum for the province. It grew to 20 pavilions with its own internal railway and thousands of patients. It was the setting of the most famous Italian identity mystery: in 1926–27 a man with no memory held here was claimed by two families, one saying he was a missing professor and the other a petty criminal. The "Collegno amnesiac" filled newspapers for years and became a byword in Italian.

The walls came down after 1978, when the Basaglia law ordered the closure of Italy's asylums, and the grounds became a public park. Some pavilions are now offices and schools; others are empty and fenced.
The park is open daily. Local volunteer guides (Ciceroni Collegnesi) give free tours. Don't go into the abandoned pavilions. Pair it with Piossasco or FATA.
collegno.s: FAI Luoghi del Cuore; TorinoToday; Mole24; general history

p: In the 18th-century cellars of the first Martini & Rossi plant at Pessione, under 30 km from Turin, a museum of wine-making with old stills, presses and vessels. Plant tours are also offered.

Martini & Rossi was founded in the 1860s and made Turin-style vermouth a global drink; its red ball-and-bar logo is one of the most recognised brands in the world. Vermouth is a Turin invention, wine flavoured with herbs and spices (see the Carpano plaque).
Online booking required; older listings give €9 (€6 reduced).

A small mountain station at 2,286 metres above Sauze d'Oulx, where a stone base carries a timber upper part with a dramatic projecting roof. Carlo Mollino built it in 1946–47 as the top station of a sled lift (slittovia), which pulled sleds full of skiers up the slope. Alpine farmhouse and modernist structure meet in one small building.

Mollino, who later built the Teatro Regio, was a passionate skier and wrote a ski manual. In the years after the war he designed several mountain buildings, and this is the best preserved. It was abandoned when the sled lift became an ordinary ski lift in 1964, and restored in 1999–2005.
Today it's a refuge restaurant in the ski season: you can eat lunch inside a Mollino building with the slopes outside the window.
In summer walk up from Pian della Rocca via Sportinia; in winter take the lifts. Check the season opening with the municipality (0122 858009).
lagonero.s: MiC Atlante; Comune di Sauze d'Oulx. Map pin approximate

p: A chain of forts climbing the mountainside above Val Chisone for about 3 km, joined by a covered staircase of around 4,000 steps. It is billed as the longest fortification in Europe, and from the valley it looks like a stone wall running up the mountain.

The Savoy dukes, later kings, built it from 1728 to the mid-19th century to hold the valley against France, at the time when Piedmont's border ran here. It never faced a real siege. Instead it became a prison: for political prisoners, and after 1860 for soldiers of the defeated Bourbon army of Naples. How many died there is fiercely argued, and some southern nationalist writers call it a "lager"; historians reject that claim.
Volunteers have been restoring it for decades. The long walks inside the covered staircase are the strange part: a staircase inside a tunnel inside a mountain.

Visits are guided only, booked by phone. Routes take about 1, 3 or 7 hours; the long "Passeggiata Reale" costs €20. Autumn and winter hours are reported as Mon and Thu–Sun 10–17; another listing says 9–17, so confirm. The Pragelato ski jumps are further up the same valley.
fenestrelle.s: Fortress listings (Jul 2026); general history. Map pin approximate

p: A fortress clinging to a rock above the Val di Susa, rebuilt to its present form around 1818–30, with long galleries, a great moat and underground passages. You see it from the road and the railway on the way to the French border.

The site was fortified for centuries because it controls the valley road. It belonged to France until 1708, and in 1681–87 its prisoner was the "Man in the Iron Mask", the mysterious inmate whose identity has fascinated people since Voltaire. The French razed it in 1796, and Piedmont rebuilt it in 1818–29. It now houses a section of the National Mountain Museum.
The 2026 season ran 20 June–27 September (€5, guided €8); otherwise it's closed until summer 2027.
exilles.s: forteexilles.it; general history; Turismo Torino; Fondazione Artea. Map pin approximate

p: A massive concrete gravity dam at 1,572 metres in the Gran Paradiso National Park: 52 metres high, with a crest 302 metres long, holding back Lake Ceresole. It was built in 1925–31 and inaugurated on 2 August 1931. Behind it the mountains rise straight to the glaciers.

It is the start of a hydroelectric chain built for Turin's electricity. Above it, on the road to the Nivolet pass at over 2,000 metres, the Serrù (1951) and Agnel dams store more water. Down the valley, the Rosone power station turns it into power: Iren says the whole Orco system produces about 720 GWh a year. Gran Paradiso, created in 1922 to protect the ibex, was Italy's first national park, so this is industry built inside protected nature.
The high road to Serrù and Agnel is one of the great Alpine drives, but it is closed in winter, so those dams are a summer trip.
The dam and lake are visible all year. Interior visits happen only at Iren events (Dam Day). It's a long day trip from Turin; there's little public transport.
ceresole.s: Iren; Unione Montana Gran Paradiso; Quotidiano Canavese. Map pin approximate

moncenisio.t: Mont-Cenis: dam and Vallo Alpino forts
p: At the Mont Cenis pass, a huge earth-and-rock dam 1.4 km long holds back a high Alpine lake. Around it, in the grass, are the concrete strongpoints of the Vallo Alpino, Mussolini's version of the Maginot line (1933–42): cave works dug into the rock, firing slits and steel cupolas.

Mont Cenis was for centuries a main route between France and Italy; Napoleon built the road over it. The plateau was Italian until 1947, when the peace treaty moved the border and gave it to France as a punishment for Italy's war, forts included. EDF then built the dam in 1962–69, 120 metres high and billed as its largest rockfill dam; it drowned the old hospice of the pass under the lake. The reservoir is shared, roughly four-fifths French and one-fifth Italian.

So you stand on French soil among Italian forts that faced France, beside a French dam. The forts are open but entered entirely at your own risk; bring a torch, stay on paths and treat interiors as unsafe. Start from Piana delle Fontanette (2,093 m).
The pass is closed in winter, so this is a summer trip, by car.
moncenisio.s: SIOUH; Structurae; Vallo Alpino guides; EDF. Map pin approximate

stura.t: Valle Stura Vallo Alpino and Vinadio
p: Mussolini's Vallo Alpino forts in the Valle Stura near Cuneo: Opera 5 "San Membotto", one of the largest, with the only mortar block on the western Alps, plus works and barracks along the trails. The Forte di Vinadio, built by King Carlo Alberto in the 1830s–40s, runs a guided route into a 19th-century fort turned 20th-century command cave.
The Vallo Alpino was a line of concrete bunkers built along the border with France in the 1930s. In June 1940 Italy attacked France through these valleys, and the forts saw a few days of war.
Well outside the Turin area: a long day trip.
stura.s: Unione Montana Valle Stura. Map pin approximate

p: An 1878 wool mill in the Biella hills that closed in 1964, sat empty for 20 years and was revived in 1984 as a museum. It keeps its water-power transmission, the shafts and belts that drove the machines from a water wheel, period machinery and about 2 km of industrial archives.
The valleys of Biella have made fine wool cloth for centuries, and the big Italian luxury brands still buy it here. The "Strada della Lana", the Wool Road, links the mills.
Open summer Sundays (June–October) 14:30–18:30, €5; after October by appointment only (351 3902199). In autumn there is a night walk along the workers' paths.
pray.s: Fabbrica della Ruota / DocBi. Map pin approximate

p: Look closely at the bronze reliefs on the base of the equestrian statue in the middle of Piazza San Carlo. On the panel showing the Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis there is a small dent: a bullet mark from the night of 22 September 1864, when soldiers fired into a crowd in this square. Almost nobody notices it.

The statue, by Carlo Marochetti (1838), shows Duke Emanuele Filiberto sheathing his sword after his victory at Saint-Quentin; Turin calls it the "Caval ëd Bronz", the bronze horse. The Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis (1559) gave him back his lands, and in 1563 he moved his capital from Chambéry to Turin. That is the founding moment of Turin as a capital, which makes the bullet's target a little ironic.

Three centuries later Turin was the capital of the new Kingdom of Italy, but in September 1864 the government agreed with France to move the capital to Florence. Turin took to the streets. On 21 September cadets fired on demonstrators in Piazza Castello, and the next night here. The government fell within a week. A plaque placed by the city in 1999 on the arcade pillar at no. 161 gives 52 dead and 187 wounded; later counts give between 55 and 62 dead. It has been called the first state massacre of united Italy.
The city lays a wreath every 21 September. It is Turin's closest equivalent to the bullet holes of Athens. The 2017 plaque and the brass bull are in the same square.

On a traffic island at a busy junction stands a bronze priest holding out a crucifix to a condemned man. This is Saint Giuseppe Cafasso, the "gallows priest", and the statue is on the exact spot where Turin's public gallows stood from 1835 to the early 1850s. The roundabout is still called the Rondò della Forca, the gallows roundabout, though the name was never official.

Executions were moved here, then open country near the prison, from Via Giulio, Piazza delle Erbe and Piazza San Carlo. Cafasso, a priest of the nearby Consolata, made it his mission to accompany the condemned: he walked with 57 men to the scaffold and is said to have never lost one to despair. He was also the mentor of Don Bosco, whose Valdocco oratory for poor boys is a few hundred metres away. Sources disagree on when hangings stopped here: 1852–53, or as late as 1863–64.

The 1960 statue by Virgilio Audagna was requested by Italy's prisoners. Turin's last hangman, Piero Pantoni, is said to have lived at Via Bonelli 2 with a wife who never went out for shame; that comes only from a blog and popular rumour. The "black magic triangle" stories are tourist esoterica.
The Museo Diffuso, the Arsenale plaque and the Martinetto are close, making this the densest cluster of memory sites on the map.

A quiet square with Cavour's statue in the middle and no marker of any kind. Its official name is Piazza Carlo Emanuele II; everyone calls it Carlina. Under French rule (1798–1814) it was renamed Place de la Liberté, and the guillotine stood roughly where Cavour now stands. 423 executions are reported for 1800–1814.

It was also next to the old Jewish ghetto, created in 1679, where Turin's Jews had to live until emancipation in 1848. You can still see it in the buildings: the corner building at Via des Ambrois has four floors plus a mezzanine in the height where its neighbours have two or three, the crowding of the ghetto written into a façade.

At no. 15, now an NH hotel, a 1957 plaque says "Here Antonio Gramsci lived in the years 1919–21", the years of *L'Ordine Nuovo* and the factory councils. The Fondazione Gramsci has display windows on the façade.
carlina.s: Istoreto; Atlante di Torino; ANPI MEMO. Map pin approximate

p: At the corner of Corso Svizzera and Corso Appio Claudio, behind a wall, is a small rifle range: a strip of ground with a stone post on the parapet and a plaque with 59 names, each with the person's job. Between 1943 and 1945 this was where Fascist firing squads shot partisans in Turin. It's now the Sacrario, the shrine, of the Martinetto.

After Italy's armistice in September 1943, the Germans occupied the north and set up Mussolini's puppet Republic of Salò. Special courts tried captured partisans and sentenced them to death, and the old army range here was the place of execution. The most famous day was 5 April 1944, when eight members of the first Piedmont military committee of the Resistance, led by General Giuseppe Perotti, were shot after a trial; the story goes that Perotti gave the order to stand to attention himself. A plaque to four of them is on Via Luini 90.

The exact number of victims differs by source: 59, "over 60", or 61. The first plaque with the names was unveiled on 8 July 1945, two months after the liberation, with the mayor and the cardinal present. Reading the professions on the plaque (workers, students, officers, a priest) shows how wide the Resistance was.
A ceremony is held every year in early April. Access times aren't confirmed, so check with the Museo Diffuso. Pian del Lot, in the hills, is the other main execution site.

A granite monument in a clearing on the road up to the Colle della Maddalena, in the hills above Turin. On 2 April 1944, 27 prisoners were taken from Le Nuove prison, brought here, shot together and buried in a common grave. On the back of the monument, the first small municipal plaque still shows the uncertainty about who some of the dead were.

It was a reprisal: two days earlier partisans had killed Ather Capelli, a Fascist newspaper editor, and the authorities chose prisoners to answer for it. The bodies were exhumed on 27 May 1945, a month after the liberation, and identified one by one.

In the city a plaque at Via Gramegna 11 was put up in 1945 by a group of neighbourhood friends, the "cricca del Moro", for five of their own killed here. It's a rare memorial made by people rather than the state.
Outdoors and always open; you need a car or bus. Commemoration every 2 April.

A street plaque at Via Cibrario 1 that begins "In this place the Nazi-Fascist lead cut short the flourishing youth…". It marks the exact spot where nine partisans, two of them Frenchmen whose names were never known, were shot on 12 October 1944.

Turin has hundreds of these "in questo luogo" plaques, mostly put up in the first years after the war by neighbourhood committees. They mark where people fell, in the street, rather than where they are buried, so the city is covered in small points of memory that most people walk past. Another plaque for nine people shot is on Piazza Statuto, a few hundred metres away.
Read the names, then look at the ordinary street around it. The 1922 plaque in Piazza XVIII Dicembre is about 300 m away.
cibrario1.s: ANPI MEMO; Atlante delle stragi. Map pin approximate

p: A plaque on the corner of Via Cernaia, opposite the old Porta Susa station, for the "Turin massacre" of 18–20 December 1922. In three days the Fascist squads of Piero Brandimarte killed 11 people, among them the communist councillor Carlo Berruti, burned the Camera del Lavoro (the trade union house) and wrecked the offices of *L'Ordine Nuovo*.

It came two months after Mussolini's March on Rome. Turin was the most "red" city in Italy, with its factory councils and communist newspaper, and the squads set out to break it. Brandimarte boasted about the killings; he was convicted in 1950 and acquitted on appeal in 1952. The square took the date as its name in 1946.
A second plaque is in the metro station's north entrance (2006); there is a ceremony every 18 December.
xviiidic.s: MuseoTorino; Consiglio Regionale; Il Caffè Torinese. Map pin approximate

p: A plaque at Via Po 46 for Roberto Crescenzio, a 22-year-old student. On 1 October 1977 masked militants who had split off from a far-left march threw Molotov cocktails into the Angelo Azzurro bar, wrongly believing it was a neo-fascist hangout. He was trapped inside, badly burned, and died two days later.

1977 was the most violent year of Italy's "years of lead", the decade of left- and right-wing terrorism. Crescenzio wasn't political; he was in the wrong bar. Four people were convicted. For decades there was no marker, until the city and the association of terrorism victims unveiled this plaque in 2017.
The place is a bar again today. Casalegno's doorway, from six weeks later, is also on this map.

A private doorway on Corso Re Umberto where, on 16 November 1977, the Red Brigades shot Carlo Casalegno, deputy editor of La Stampa, in the face. He died thirteen days later, the first journalist killed by the BR.

Casalegno had written against terrorism and in defence of the state, and Turin was the Red Brigades' main base, with Fiat their target. His son Andrea, then involved in the far-left movement, later wrote about his father's death and about the fact that nothing on the street recalls it; the only plaque is inside the La Stampa building.
This is a spot, not a sight. Stand for a moment and move on.
casalegno.s: Andrea Casalegno, Anni spietati. Map pin approximate

micca.t: Pietro Micca museum and siege tunnels
p: A museum of the 1706 siege, and below it the real thing: you go down to 6 and then 14 metres into the counter-mine tunnels the defenders dug under the citadel, lit by lanterns, to the stair Pietro Micca ran down and the spot where his body was found. This is the most physical history site in Turin.

In 1706 a French army besieged Turin for four months. Above ground there was bombardment; underground, a second war: the French dug tunnels toward the citadel to blow up its walls, and the Piedmontese dug counter-tunnels to find and destroy them. On the night of 29–30 August French grenadiers broke into a gallery. Micca, a miner, and his companion were ordered to blow it up; legend says he sent his companion away, lit a short fuse and could not get clear. He saved the citadel, and his body was found in the tunnel.

A week later, on 7 September, the siege was broken. The original tunnel network ran about 21 km; you see about 400 m. The "Pietro Micca stair" was found bricked up in 1958 by Captain Guido Amoretti, who spent his life excavating the tunnels. The 1961 museum building stands where a French battery shelled the citadel.

Open Tue–Sun 10–18 (last entry 17). The tunnels must be booked (011 01167580) and run at 10:30, 14:30 and 16:30, plus 15:30 on Sundays. Cheap; Abbonamento Musei valid. A plaque to the siege dead is round the corner at Via Amoretti 7/A, and the Mastio is a few minutes away. Superga was built to give thanks for this victory.

A massive brick keep with cannons outside, at the corner of Corso Galileo Ferraris and Via Cernaia. It is the Mastio, the main gate-tower of the 1564 pentagonal citadel, and the only piece left of the fortress that held out in the siege of 1706. Look at its front entrance: it's a fake door, and the grimacing mask on the keystone is said to be there to mock invaders.

Duke Emanuele Filiberto built the citadel when he made Turin his capital. It was one of the most advanced fortresses in Europe, a five-pointed star with tunnels underneath (the ones you visit at the Pietro Micca museum). In the 19th century the city needed space, and the citadel was demolished in 1856 except for this keep.

Since 1896 it has held the national artillery museum and now hosts exhibitions; in 2026 it opened a new underground archaeological area. Hours are irregular, so check before going; the outside is always visible.

On the corner of Via Verdi and Via Montebello stand the outer walls of a theatre, roofless, with part of the foyer still there. The 1857 Teatro Scribe, later Teatro di Torino, was gutted by bombs on 8 December 1942 and never rebuilt. The Resistance institute calls it the only conspicuous visible memory of the war damage in the city.

The theatre's best years came after 1925, when Riccardo Gualino took it over. Gualino was an industrialist and one of the great art collectors of his time, a patron of avant-garde theatre, music and the Turin painters. His theatre staged modern European drama and dance that Italy rarely saw. He fell foul of Fascism and was sent into internal exile in 1931; his collection is now in the Galleria Sabauda.

December 1942 was the worst month of the bombing, when the RAF raided Turin night after night. Most damaged buildings were rebuilt, and that's what makes this one strange: a ruin left standing in the centre, a few steps from the Mole. Across the street, the RAI building at Via Verdi 16 was a barracks hit in August 1943; no scars are visible there today.
Look from the street; no entry.
teatrotorino.s: MuseoTorino; Istoreto; general history. Map pin approximate

valdofusi.t: Piazza Valdo Fusi: the bombing void
p: An open square over an underground car park, oddly empty for the middle of Turin. Before the bombs, a full city block stood here, including the old Politecnico. The emptiness itself is the war scar.

The block was destroyed in the raids of 1942–43, and for decades the gap was used as a car park and a market. In the 2000s it became a square with an underground garage. It's named after Valdo Fusi, a lawyer of the Resistance who wrote a memoir of the Turin prisons.
On Via Po, at nos. 42–44, postwar buildings fill another bomb gap inside the 18th-century arcades. The Ex Borsa and Palazzo degli Affari face this square.
valdofusi.s: Boido & Davico (Politecnico, 2023); Istoreto. Map pin approximate

p: Turin's synagogue on Via San Pio V, a Moorish-style building with four onion-topped towers. The bombing raid of 21 November 1942 gutted the interior and left only the four towers and outer walls; it was rebuilt after the war. Round the side, on Via Sant'Anselmo, the old "brides' door" at no. 7 is bricked up.

Turin's Jews had been confined to the ghetto until 1848. After emancipation they planned a grand synagogue, the building that became the Mole Antonelliana; when Antonelli's ambitions made it too costly, the community sold it to the city and built this one in 1880–84 in San Salvario. Under the 1938 racial laws and the 1943–45 occupation, many of Turin's Jews were deported; Primo Levi was one.

The story that people sifted gold from the rubble is, by the Resistance institute's own guide, a legend. The inside can be visited by booking with the Jewish Community. The walled door wasn't re-checked after 2020.

Eight tunnel mouths in the retaining wall below Monte dei Cappuccini, on Via Gaetano Giardino, six of them bricked up and one widened and gated. This is one of only two public air-raid shelters dug into Turin's hill during the war.

The hill across the Po was safe ground: solid rock, close to the centre. Inside are four cross-galleries lettered A to D. After the war some of the tunnels were reused by a space-physics institute for instruments that needed stable underground conditions.
You can read it all from the pavement; no entry. The church of Santa Maria del Monte above has cannonballs in its walls.

Four walled-up shelter entrances in Parco Leopardi on Corso Moncalieri, still marked "P.A.A." for Protezione Anti Aerea, the wartime civil defence. Like the Cappuccini tunnels, they were dug into the hill across the river.
The letters were painted in the 1940s and have survived 80 years of weather. Public park; pin approximate, so look along the slope.

On the arrivals side of Porta Nuova station, on Via Sacchi, a plaque reads: "From this station the political deportees left for the Nazi extermination camps…". Turin's main station, where millions arrived from the south to work at Fiat, was also where prisoners left for Mauthausen and Auschwitz.
After the strikes of March 1944, hundreds of Turin workers were deported to camps in Austria and Germany as punishment; many didn't come back. A one-minute stop when you pass the station.

Two small brass "stumbling stones" in the pavement outside Via Po 25, for Michele Valabrega and Maria Irene Roscetti. They were arrested on 5 December 1943, deported on the same convoy as Primo Levi and murdered at Auschwitz. Their daughter Stella survived.

The stones are the work of the German artist Gunter Demnig, who since the 1990s has placed them in front of the last homes of victims of Nazism across Europe; you "stumble" on them as you walk. Turin has about 130. At Piazza Castello 161 are the Colombo family, lured to a fake business meeting at a café on Via Roma and arrested by the SS. Others are at Corso San Maurizio 8 and Via San Domenico 0–1 (Father Girotti, who died at Dachau).
The Museo Diffuso has walking routes linking them. Look down.
inciampo.s: Museo Diffuso della Resistenza. Map pin approximate

p: In the garden of Cascina Marchesa, an old farmhouse in Barriera di Milano, stand two plaques moved from the Fiat Grandi Motori plant. One marks where five worker-partisans fell under German tank fire on 27 April 1945, quoting the poet Carducci: "and with stones one answers lead".

In the last days of April 1945, before the Allies arrived, Turin's factory workers occupied their plants to stop the Germans destroying them, and fought from inside. The Grandi Motori was one of the hardest-fought.
Public garden. Pin approximate.

The courtyard of the Museo Diffuso della Resistenza on Corso Valdocco holds plaques rescued from the Fiat Ferriere and Grandi Motori plants, recalling the factory that gave "the first spark of the revolt" of 18–28 April 1945. When the factories closed, their memorials were saved here.

The museum itself tells the story of Turin under war, occupation and Resistance; it also runs the openings of the Piazza Risorgimento shelter and the stumbling-stone walks. The building is an 18th-century barracks by Juvarra.
Courtyard generally open in museum hours. The Rondò della Forca is at the end of the street.

supergacrash.t: Superga: the Grande Torino crash wall
p: Behind the basilica of Superga, on the retaining wall at the back of the hill, is a marble plaque with a list of names. The wall still bears the mark of the impact of 4 May 1949, when the plane carrying the Grande Torino, Italy's best football team, crashed into the hill in fog. People leave scarves, flowers and maroon flags here all year.

The Grande Torino had won five league titles in a row, and the team was the pride of a country rebuilding after the war; most of the national side came from it. They were flying back from Lisbon, where they had played a friendly for the farewell of Benfica's captain. Over Turin there was rain and low cloud, with visibility near Superga down to about 40 metres. At 17:03 the Fiat G.212 hit the wall at 675 metres. All 31 on board died: 18 players, coaches, managers, three journalists and the crew. There were no black boxes, and the exact cause was never established.

Half a million people came to the funeral. Torino has never been the same club since. The basilica itself, by Juvarra (1717–31), was built to give thanks for the end of the 1706 siege, and holds the tombs of the Savoy kings. A small museum of the Grande Torino is in Grugliasco.
Free and always open on foot. Ride up on the Sassi–Superga rack tramway. The site is protected, and in 2026 the city and Torino fans signed a pact to maintain it.
supergacrash.s: Il Post; Corriere dello Sport (2024–25); Linea Italia Piemonte (Apr 2026)

p: A working hotel on Piazza Carlo Felice, opposite Porta Nuova. On 27 August 1950 Cesare Pavese was found dead in its room 346, after an overdose of sleeping pills. On the first page of a book by the bed he had written: “I forgive everyone and ask everyone's forgiveness. All right? Not too much gossip.”

He was 41 and at the height of his fame: two months earlier he had won the Strega Prize for *La bella estate*. His last diary entry, ten days before, ends "Not words. An act. I won't write any more." He chose a hotel by the station in August, when Turin was empty. The hotel's own history also notes it was hit by incendiary bombs on 8 December 1942.
No plaque outside, and the room is an ordinary guest room. Caffè Elena is the place to sit where he wrote.
pavese.s: Hotel Roma e Rocca Cavour; general literary history

p: An 1861 marble plaque on the corner of Via Lagrange and Via Cavour: Count Camillo di Cavour was born in this house on 10 August 1810 and died here on 6 June 1861. That is, three months after he had seen Italy proclaimed.

Cavour was the architect of Italian unification: a liberal aristocrat who modernised Piedmont's economy and railways and used diplomacy, an alliance with France and a war with Austria to bring Italy together under the Savoy king. He died suddenly of a fever (probably malaria) at 50; his last words are reported as "Italy is made, all is safe". His funeral was held in the church of the tiny piazzetta nearby.
Always visible. Del Cambio, where his table is kept, is a few minutes away.
cavourhouse.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026; general history. Map pin approximate

p: A small garden bed and a plaque in Largo Cibrario for the 64 people who died in the Cinema Statuto fire of 13 February 1983. A curtain caught fire during a Sunday showing of the comedy *La Capra*; most of the victims were found behind emergency exits that had been chained shut.
It was the worst cinema fire in Italian history, and it led directly to the country's modern fire-safety rules for cinemas and theatres. The owner and others were convicted.
The plaque was vandalised in 2017 and is still there. A second memorial is at the Cimitero Parco. The "evil vortex" stories online are nonsense: the fire was an accident made deadly by negligence.
statuto.s: Quotidiano Piemontese (Jan 2026); general news coverage. Map pin approximate

p: An 1886 bronze plaque on the old arsenal at Piazza Borgo Dora, now Sermig's Arsenale della Pace. It honours Sergeant Paolo Sacchi, who on 26 April 1852, after the powder magazine exploded, kept 40,000 kg of gunpowder from catching fire and so "saved Turin".

The explosion damaged every house in Borgo Dora. The death toll is disputed: 26, or 20 plus 3 who died in hospital. Sacchi became a national hero. The story that the blast blew Don Bosco's hat off, at his oratory a few streets away, is tradition.
The building has a second life: since 1983 Sermig, a Catholic lay group, has turned the military arsenal into a "peace arsenal" for the homeless and migrants. The arsenal of war became a shelter.

In April 1728 a 16-year-old Rousseau, a runaway apprentice from Geneva, was registered at the hospice for converts here as "Rosso, Gio Giacomo, of Geneva, Calvinist" and gave up his Protestant faith a week or so later. He tells the story, without flattering himself, in the *Confessions*.

He stayed in Turin for over a year, poor and drifting. He worked as a footman in Palazzo Solaro della Chiusa, now the MAO museum at Via San Domenico 11, where he stole a ribbon and let a servant girl take the blame, the guilt he said haunted him all his life.
No plaque at either place; the hospice building may not survive as such.
rousseau.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026; Rousseau, Confessions. Map pin approximate

p: In the garden of Piazza Statuto stands a 7.94-metre granite obelisk with a bronze armillary sphere on top. It isn't decoration: it was put up in 1808 on the stones that marked the Turin end of a measured line, the baseline Giovanni Battista Beccaria used to work out the size of the Earth. Its twin stands 11.8 km west at Rivoli, at the other end. Corso Francia runs almost along the line between them.

In the 18th century scientists were arguing about the shape of the Earth: was it flattened at the poles, and by how much? The answer came from measuring the length of one degree of latitude in different places. Beccaria, a physics professor (also known for his work on electricity, and a correspondent of Benjamin Franklin), measured this base in May 1760 with rods laid end to end, then built a network of triangles from it. His result, published as *Gradus Taurinensis* (1774), was 112.008 km per degree, against 111.139 today.

His error was partly real science: he noticed that the mass of the Alps was pulling his plumb line sideways, one of the first observations of the effect. Napoleon's surveyors later relied on his triangles. That's why the obelisks went up in 1808, under French rule. It is the closest thing Turin has to the standard-metre marks of Paris.

The stories about the 45th parallel or a "black magic" centre here are myth. Farmacia Almasio, on the corner of Via Manzoni, has kept its furnishings of 1868 almost intact. The Frejus monument is at the other end of the square.
beccaria.s: Sena (Politecnico di Torino); general history of geodesy

p: At the end of Corso Francia in Rivoli stands an obelisk identical to the one in Piazza Statuto, inaugurated on 8 October 1808. It marks the western end of Beccaria's 1760 baseline, 11.8 km long, the line he measured to calculate the size of the Earth. Corso Francia runs almost along it, so you can travel the whole base between the two.

Look also for a 1934 plaque set into the pavement by the newsstand at the start of Via Fratelli Piol. Beccaria extended his base up to Rivoli castle in 1762. The castle now holds Italy's leading museum of contemporary art, so you can pair 18th-century science with 20th-century art.
rivoliobelisk.s: Sena (Politecnico di Torino). Map pin approximate

p: Under the arcade on Via Po, at no. 18, a plaque reads: "In the old chemical laboratory of this building, Ascanio Sobrero… first achieved the synthesis of nitroglycerine." This is where, in 1846–47, one of the most dangerous substances in chemistry was first made.

Sobrero was a Turin chemist who had trained in Paris in the laboratory of Théophile-Jules Pelouze. He mixed glycerine with nitric and sulphuric acid and got an oily liquid that exploded at the slightest shock; it scarred his face in one accident. He was frightened by it and warned against its use. He also tasted it, as chemists did then, and noted a violent headache: that was the effect on blood vessels that makes nitroglycerine a medicine for angina to this day.

Alfred Nobel, who had also worked in Pelouze's lab and met Sobrero, found a way to make it safe to handle by soaking it into earth: dynamite (1867). It made Nobel rich and, in the end, funded the Nobel prizes. Sobrero said he felt almost ashamed to be its discoverer. Nobel's company later paid him a pension.
His monument in the Valentino, a bronze bust above a young titan tearing at rocks (1914), sits near the Borgo Medievale. The old university courtyard is across the street.
sobrero.s: MuseoTorino; Treccani; general history of chemistry

p: The former Ospizio di Carità on Via Po, a charity hospice. On 7 November 1896 Vittorio Calcina, the Lumière brothers' agent in Italy, showed about twenty short films here to an invited audience including the mayor: trains arriving, workers leaving a factory, a gardener sprayed with his own hose. It is often billed as Italy's first public film show, but Calcina had already shown the Lumière films in Milan on 29 March 1896, so treat "first" as disputed.

The Lumières had shown their first films to a paying public in Paris in December 1895. Calcina then filmed Turin himself, the royal family and street scenes. What Turin can fairly claim is one of Italy's earliest permanent cinemas: the room ran as the "Kinematografo Lumière" until March 1897, when shows moved to a beer hall on Via Garibaldi.

It's the first chapter of a big story: within fifteen years Turin was Italy's film capital, with the Ambrosio and Itala studios making epics for the world. That's why the National Cinema Museum is in the Mole. There's no plaque; you see the façade.
lumiere.s: MuseoTorino; general history; Wikipedia (Vittorio Calcina); victorian-cinema.net. Map pin approximate

p: The old university of 1714–20 on Via Po, with an arcaded courtyard on two levels, built when Vittorio Amedeo II reformed the university. Beccaria taught physics here from 1748, and Lagrange studied here.

On the night of 25–26 January 1904 a fire broke out in the National Library, then housed in the building, and burned five rooms, destroying much of its great manuscript collection, including medieval codices from the Bobbio monastery. Libraries and governments around the world sent donations.

The chemist Icilio Guareschi worked for years to save fused and blackened parchments, and in doing so effectively founded the chemistry of library conservation. The courtyard is usually open on weekdays; the Sobrero plaque is across the street.
unipo.s: MuseoTorino; BNU Torino; RSUT (2019). Map pin approximate

p: Look up at the west tower of Palazzo Madama, the castle in the middle of Piazza Castello. From 1822 to 1912 it was Turin's astronomical observatory, with a rotating dome on top and, from 1885, a 30 cm refractor telescope.

The astronomer Giovanni Plana moved the observatory here. It worked well until the 1890s, when the city's new electric street lights flooded the sky, an early case of light pollution killing science. The observatory moved out to Pino Torinese in the hills, where it still is, and the dome was demolished in 1920.

Palazzo Madama itself is a stack of history: a Roman gate, a medieval castle and a Baroque façade by Juvarra. Nothing of the observatory survives here, so this is a look-up-and-imagine stop. The earlier observatory on the Academy of Sciences' top floor (1790) does survive and reopened in 2026.
specola.s: Schiavone; INAF; general history. Map pin approximate

p: A two-storey office block on the Dora riverbank, and behind it a glass-roofed film stage 50 by 25 metres on iron pillars. This was the studio of Ambrosio Film, Italy's biggest silent-film company, built by Pietro Fenoglio in 1911–13. The façade is unchanged.

Arturo Ambrosio founded the company in 1906–07. Films then needed daylight, hence the glass roof. Ambrosio made *The Last Days of Pompeii* (1908 and 1913) and other epics that were shown worldwide; the studio had over 75 actors and 400 staff. Fenoglio was Turin's master of Art Nouveau, so even a film factory got elegance.

When Hollywood took over the world market after the First World War, Turin's studios collapsed; during the war Ambrosio made aircraft propellers, and it went bankrupt in 1924. The building is now Teatro Espace and a café. Its earlier 1909 stage was round the corner at Via Catania 30.

The site of Itala Film's studios, built here in 1906–15. Giovanni Pastrone made *Cabiria* here in 1914: a three-hour epic of the Punic Wars, with intertitles by D'Annunzio, huge sets of Carthage and the first famous use of a moving camera dolly, the "carrello". It influenced D. W. Griffith and the first Hollywood epics.

*Cabiria* also created Maciste, the strongman who went on to star in dozens of films. Whether any studio building survives is unconfirmed, so this is a look-from-the-street stop. The Cinema Museum in the Mole has *Cabiria*'s sets and posters.
itala.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026; general film history. Map pin approximate

p: A working cinema inside the Galleria Subalpina, the 1870s glass-and-iron arcade off Piazza Castello. A Lumière projection room opened in the basement in 1905, and the arcade has been showing films ever since.

The cinema calls itself Italy's first art-house cinema; that's disputed (art-house programming started in 1971). The Galleria itself is one of the finest arcades in Italy, modelled on the Paris passages, and Nietzsche walked through it daily from his room at the other end.
A good place to actually see a film in a historic setting.
romano.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026. Map pin approximate

p: Long brick factory buildings on Corso Dante, now converted into lofts. This was Fiat's first factory, built in 1899–1900 just after the company was founded. It's where Turin's car industry started, before the Lingotto and Mirafiori.

Fiat (Fabbrica Italiana Automobili Torino) was founded in July 1899 by a group of Turin aristocrats and businessmen, among them Giovanni Agnelli, who soon took control. The first cars were built here, a few dozen a year at first. By the First World War Fiat was making trucks, aircraft engines and machine guns, and had outgrown the site.

In September 1920, during the "red two years" after the war, workers occupied the factories of northern Italy and ran them themselves for a month through factory councils. Antonio Gramsci, writing in *L'Ordine Nuovo*, saw the councils as the seeds of a new state, and Corso Dante was one of the centres of the occupation. It ended in a compromise, and two years later the Fascists were in power. The plant was bombed on 8 December 1942.
No plaque. Look at the buildings from Corso Dante and the river side. The founding deed was signed at Palazzo Bricherasio, and Gramsci's lodging plaque is on Piazza Carlina.

Palazzo Cacherano di Bricherasio on Via Lagrange, where Fiat's founding deed was signed in July 1899 (the date is disputed, 1 or 11 July). Count Emanuele Cacherano di Bricherasio was one of the founders, and the meeting was held in his home.

Outside, the only plaque is for the poet Giovanni Berchet; inside hangs a copy of Lorenzo Delleani's painting of the signing, with Giovanni Agnelli among the founders. Bricherasio died mysteriously in 1904, and some suspected he had been pushed out of the company.
It's now a bank, so outside only except during events.
bricherasio.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026; general history. Map pin approximate

p: Under the arcades at Piazza Castello and Via Viotti, a plaque says that in 1786 Antonio Benedetto Carpano created his vermouth "in this house". His shop here is documented; that he invented vermouth is tradition.

Vermouth is white wine flavoured with herbs and spices (the name comes from the German for wormwood). Carpano's shop, open almost round the clock, became one of the city's meeting places, and vermouth became the ritual drink of the Turin aperitivo, which this city claims to have invented.
Check the plaque in person; its date is unknown. To drink one in context, go to Caffè Elena, where the Carpano firm is said to have refined the recipe, or visit Casa Martini.

A public bench painted black and white, with a plaque, at Corso Re Umberto and Corso Vittorio Emanuele II. Juventus was founded on a bench here in 1897 by students of the Liceo d'Azeglio, who chose the Latin name for youth. This one is a stand-in, repainted in July 2025 and placed opposite the original spot.

The club's first shirts were pink; the black-and-white stripes came in 1903 when a member had shirts sent from Notts County in England. Juventus became Italy's most successful club, owned by the Agnelli family since 1923. The real bench has been in the J Museum since 2012, and the first club meetings were held in the Canfari brothers' workshop at Corso Re Umberto 42.
Torino FC, the rival club, was founded in Bar Norman nine years later; both are on this map.
juvebench.s: Torino Cronaca; Juventus. Map pin approximate

p: Torino FC was founded on the mezzanine of this bar, then the Birreria Voigt, on 3 December 1906, by members of Football Club Torinese and a group of Juventus dissidents led by the Swiss Alfred Dick. A plaque and a photo of the founders hang inside.

Dick had been Juventus's president and wanted to make it more professional, and the split created the derby. Ever since, Torino has been the club of the old working city and Juventus the club of the Agnellis. The Grande Torino of the 1940s and the crash at Superga made Torino a legend.
Have a drink where the derby began.
norman.s: Torino FC history. Map pin approximate

p: A lone brick chimney in Parco Dora, from the stamping shops of Michelin's first Italian plant, opened in 1906. Everything else of the factory is gone.

The French tyre-maker came to Turin because the car industry was here: Fiat, Lancia, Itala and dozens of smaller makers. For a century this stretch of the Dora was lined with factories. Now the chimney stands in a park, next to the steel skeletons of the Fiat steelworks and Botta's church, which kept another chimney as its bell tower.
michelin.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026. Map pin approximate

p: A faded plaque, hard to read, at Via Lagrange 29: "Giuseppe Luigi Lagrange was born in this house on 25 January 1736." He became one of the greatest mathematicians of all time, and Turin's most famous scientist.

He taught at Turin's artillery school as a teenager and co-founded the society that became the Academy of Sciences. Then he left: Frederick the Great called him to Berlin, and later he moved to Paris, where he chaired the commission that created the metric system and is buried in the Panthéon. His *Analytical Mechanics* recast physics in pure mathematics; the Lagrangian and Lagrange points are named after him.
His statue (1867) stands nearby in Piazza Lagrange. The Academy and the metric connection (see the Beccaria obelisk) are part of the same story.
lagrange.s: Torino Cronaca; general history of science. Map pin approximate

p: Three 19th-century museums in one university building: Luigi Rolando's anatomy rooms with their old wooden cases, wax and papier-mâché models and preparations; Cesare Lombroso's museum of criminal anthropology, with skulls, criminals' death masks, weapons and the drawings and objects made by inmates; and Francesco Garnier Valletti's hundreds of artificial fruits, made to teach pomology.

Lombroso was a Turin doctor and one of the most famous scientists of the late 19th century. He claimed that criminals were "born", a throwback to earlier humans, and could be recognised by the shape of their skulls and faces. His theory shaped police and courts across Europe and gave scientific cover to prejudice, especially against southern Italians. It has long been discredited. The museum, reopened in 2009, presents it as a case study in how science can go wrong. In a final display, Lombroso's own skeleton is on show; he left his body to his museum.

The museum has been controversial: activists from Calabria went to court for years to get back the skull of Giuseppe Villella, which Lombroso used as the founding evidence of his theory. The anatomy museum (founded 1739) is the opposite: a beautifully preserved room of real 19th-century science.
Open Mon–Sat 10–18 (last entry 17:30). Three-museum ticket €10 (€6 reduced). The fruit museum's entrance is on Corso Massimo d'Azeglio 52.
anatomici.s: Museo di Anatomia Umana; Museo Lombroso; general history

p: A pharmacy trading since 1667, the Regia Farmacia Masino, with 18th-century wooden fittings, its original ceramic jars and a bronze mortar dated 1718. It's still a working pharmacy.

"Regia" means it had a royal licence: it supplied the court. Turin keeps several such historic pharmacies (Anglesio, Almasio, Consolata), with their shelving, jars and counters intact. They're among the oldest shop interiors in the city.
Step in during shop hours and buy something small.
A pharmacy in the same family since 1682, with a big historic sign and its original fittings. Shop hours.

Turin's old pharmacies were part laboratory, making medicines on the spot from herbs and chemicals; the jars and drawers were their stock. Nearby, the Farmacia della Consolata (Via delle Orfane 25) has fittings MuseoTorino calls unique; its "since 1510" is marketing.

A 1949 plaque signed "Turin remembers" on Via dell'Arcivescovado 7. The building held the Piedmont edition of the socialist *Avanti!* and the rooms where *L'Ordine Nuovo* was written: the weekly founded on 1 May 1919 by Antonio Gramsci, Palmiro Togliatti, Angelo Tasca and Umberto Terracini.

*L'Ordine Nuovo* argued that the factory councils of Turin's workers could be the basis of a new socialist state, and it became the seed of the Italian Communist Party, founded in 1921. The Fascists wrecked its offices in December 1922. Later the building held the first offices of Einaudi, the publishing house of Pavese, Levi and Calvino.
Gramsci's lodging plaque is on Piazza Carlina.
ordinenuovo.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026; general history. Map pin approximate

teatronuovo.t: Teatro Nuovo: the march of the 40,000
p: On 14 October 1980, day 35 of the strike that had blocked Fiat, a meeting of foremen and white-collar staff at this theatre overflowed into a silent march through the city to the town hall: the "march of the 40,000". Within hours the unions signed an agreement and the strike ended.

Fiat had announced thousands of layoffs, and the unions had blockaded the gates of Mirafiori for five weeks. The march showed that many employees wanted to go back to work. Crowd estimates range from 12,000 to 40,000. It's remembered as the end of the era of factory militancy that began in 1969, and a turning point for Italian unions.
There's no plaque. The Mirafiori factory is the other end of the story.
teatronuovo.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026; general history. Map pin approximate

p: The buildings of an asbestos-cement factory that ran from 1911 to 1952, listed in a 1984 census as "of documentary interest".

Asbestos was a miracle material for roofs and pipes, and Piedmont was its Italian heartland: the Eternit plant at Casale Monferrato, east of Turin, made the region the centre of Italy's asbestos tragedy, with thousands of deaths. This is a smaller, earlier piece of that story. Current state unconfirmed; outside only.
An IEEE Milestone plaque for Galileo Ferraris, who discovered the rotating magnetic field in 1885, the principle behind most electric motors in the world today. It was dedicated in 2021.

Ferraris, a professor in Turin, built a small motor based on two alternating currents out of phase, and chose not to patent it, believing science should be free. Nikola Tesla reached the same idea independently, and Westinghouse bought Tesla's patents; the priority dispute lasted years. Ferraris also founded Italy's first school of electrical engineering here in 1888.

Where the plaque is now is unclear. IEEE lists the Energy Center (Via Borsellino 38/16, entrance hall), but a 2024 Politecnico release puts it with a new bust in the atrium of Sala "Emma Strada" on the main campus. Check both.
ferraris.s: IEEE / ETHW; Politecnico di Torino (2024). Map pin approximate

p: Luigi Lavazza's grocery of 1895 at Via San Tommaso 10, where he started buying coffee from different countries and blending it, the idea that built the brand. It's now the "San Tommaso 10" café and restaurant, with company-history photos on the walls.

Lavazza is still a Turin family company and one of the world's biggest coffee roasters; espresso as Italians drink it was largely shaped by Turin firms and Turin inventions (the first espresso machine patent was filed here in 1884). Have an espresso where it started.
lavazza.s: Lavazza; Michelin guide. Map pin approximate

p: The corner of Via Ormea and Via Donizetti in San Salvario, where Vincenzo Lancia, a former Fiat racing driver, founded his car company on 27 November 1906. A fire in 1907 destroyed the first prototype, and the workshop doors are said to have been widened to get the first car out.

Lancia became Italy's most inventive car maker: the Lambda of 1922 had the first unitary body and independent front suspension, and later Lancias won rallies for decades. The company later moved to Borgo San Paolo, where its tower still stands. Fiat took it over in 1969. No plaque: a spot only.
lancia.s: ACS Epoca (2012); general history. Map pin approximate

p: A grass airfield on Corso Francia, still in use by the Aero Club Torino. On 22 May 1917 the test pilot Mario De Bernardi took off from here, then the field of the Pomilio aircraft company, in a Pomilio PC1 biplane bound for Rome, carrying 200 kg of mail. For the flight the post office overprinted a stamp: the world's first airmail stamp, now a famous rarity.

Turin was the cradle of Italian aviation. The first aerodrome was at Mirafiori (now Parco Colonnetti), one of Italy's biggest early flying schools, and Fiat and other firms built aircraft engines here from the 1910s. Leonardo's aircraft division is still on Corso Francia, next to the field.
Look through the fence at the small planes. Collectors call the 1917 stamp the "Pomilio".

The university's botanic garden, founded in 1729 as a royal garden next to the Valentino castle. In its "Boschetto", a small wood, stand an old Ginkgo, a cedar and a yew, and the greenhouses hold collections built up over three centuries.

It was a teaching garden for medicine, when doctors had to know their plants. Its iconography collection, the Iconographia Taurinensis, is a series of thousands of botanical paintings made for the court from the 18th century. A new railing (2025) lets passers-by see in.
Open late March to mid-November, Sat 14:30–19, Sun 10–19 (2025 schedule), €5. Closed for the season from about 17 November.
ortobot.s: Turismo Torino; Artribune. Map pin approximate

p: The regional natural science museum, in the former San Giovanni hospital, a huge 17th-century building in the centre. Its collections range from minerals to whale skeletons.
