In August 2013 a small explosion in the building's service area closed the museum, and it stayed shut for more than ten years, a long-running embarrassment for the region. It partly reopened in January 2024, and more works were approved in October 2026, so check what's open before you go.
scienzenat.s: Regione Piemonte; mentelocale (Jan 2026). Map pin approximate

p: Corso Re Umberto 75: Primo Levi was born in this house in 1919 and died here in 1987, falling down the stairwell. His surname is still on the doorbell. He spent almost his whole life in this building, apart from one year: 1944, at Auschwitz.

Levi was a chemist. He joined a partisan band in 1943, was captured, identified as a Jew and deported. *If This Is a Man* (1947) is one of the essential books about the camps. He went back to work as a chemist in a paint factory, and wrote *The Periodic Table*, each chapter named after an element. Whether his death was suicide or an accident is still argued.

Rita Levi-Montalcini, the Nobel neurobiologist, ran her secret bedroom laboratory on the same street in 1940 (number unknown). The Primo Levi study centre is in Via del Carmine. A spot to stop, not a sight; a plaque is not confirmed.
primolevi.s: The Spectator; studenti.it; general history. Map pin approximate

p: A workers' mutual-aid society that still meets: SOMS "Edmondo De Amicis" on Corso Casale. Inside, Turin's SOMS clubs keep banners, members' photos and old documents on the walls; one is said to have a letter from Garibaldi.

The Società Operaie di Mutuo Soccorso were founded from the 1850s by workers who paid small dues to help each other in sickness, injury and old age: the welfare system of the working class before the state had one. Piedmont had hundreds. Many survive as social clubs with a bar, a hall and bocce.
Go in as a guest of the bar if it's open, and look at the walls.
soms.s: Gambero Rosso (Jul 2026); Regione Piemonte. Map pin approximate

p: A little Liberty-era urinal kiosk in front of the pharmacy on Piazza Villari, cast in "artificial stone" and stamped "U. Renzi". It is one of the two oldest survivors of Turin's historic public urinals, and since 2023–24 it has been painted pastel green and pink as a street-art piece.

In the 1870s–80s the hygienist Giacinto Pacchiotti campaigned for Paris-style urinals to replace the "decency stones" men used against walls. The Turin firm of Umberto Renzi moved from iron kiosks to cast stone, and its curved 1930s "Modello '900" spread across Italy and its colonies. About 29 Renzi urinals survive among the city's 190 public toilets; the city wants to keep 13 as historic objects, and the rest are being demolished one by one. It's the Turin cousin of the last Paris vespasienne.
Mostly locked or tagged: things to look at, not to use. Others on the map: Piazza Sassari (the other Liberty one), Corso Regina Margherita 103 and Corso Massimo d'Azeglio 16.

The other Liberty-style Renzi urinal: a pierced cast-stone kiosk on little columns near Via Cigna, made by the Turin firm that supplied half of Italy's public urinals. With Piazza Villari's, it's one of the two oldest that survive.
The pierced design let air through and hid the user from the waist up, the same idea as the Paris vespasiennes. Condition not re-checked in 2026.

A classic 1930s Renzi "Modello '900" urinal in front of Corso Regina Margherita 103, near the Giardini Reali. This curved concrete kiosk was the standard Italian urinal for decades, made in Turin and installed from Bolzano to the colonies in Africa.
It's tagged but intact. With the Liberty ones in Piazza Villari and Piazza Sassari, it shows how the design changed from ornament to streamlined modern.
Another Renzi "Modello '900" kiosk, on the side road in front of Corso Massimo d'Azeglio 16, just before the Teatro Nuovo. The city lists it among the historic urinals it intends to keep.
Turin's old urinals are disappearing fast: those in Corso Marconi and Corso Tazzoli are already gone. Seeing one intact is a small piece of luck.

A modest Liberty-style building of 1901 at the corner of Corso Regina Margherita and Via Vanchiglia, that still does the job it was built for: public baths, where people without a bathroom at home come for a hot shower. Volunteers from the Alpini civil protection run it, and it had 7,478 visits in 2022.

At the end of the 19th century most working-class flats in Turin had no bathroom, and many had no running water. Hygienists pushed the city to build public baths ("bagni popolari"), first on the Po in summer, then shower buildings in each district so people could wash all year for a few cents. The city engineer Camillo Dolza designed many of them in the early 1900s. This one was lightly damaged in July 1943 and is one of the few that keeps both its original building and its original use.
It's a reminder that "no bathroom" isn't ancient history: people still come here because they need to.
Respect it as a working service. Other baths on the map: Via Morgari (the prettiest, now a café), San Donato (a library), Via Agliè and Via Cherasco (still working).

In San Salvario, a low Liberty building with curving wings and a cornice of alternating frogs and shells, a fitting decoration for a building made for water. It was built as public baths in the early 1900s, designed by the city engineer Camillo Dolza, and is now the Casa del Quartiere: a café, community centre and events space.

Turin built a network of these "bagni popolari" around 1900 for working-class districts where flats had no bathrooms. San Salvario was then a crowded neighbourhood of workers and small trades by the railway. Dolza gave even a shower house a bit of Art Nouveau elegance, as if to say that hygiene deserved beauty too.

Today San Salvario is Turin's multicultural, nightlife district, and the old baths have become its living room. The conversion kept the building and gave it a new public use, which is the best fate these buildings have had.
Have a coffee, look up at the frogs, and compare it with the still-working baths in Vanchiglia.

A 1900 building in Borgo San Donato that held the district's first shower baths (later 40 tubs), a wash-house decorated with animal motifs, and the custodian's house. It's now the Gabriele d'Annunzio public library.

Women came to the wash-house to do the family laundry in big stone tubs, and men and women came to the baths on separate days. These buildings were small temples of public hygiene, and the decoration shows the city was proud of them.
Go in to the library and look at the old structure.
A working 1956 municipal bathhouse in Barriera di Milano, one of the poorest districts. It replaced baths housed in an old customs house on Piazza Crispi, which was demolished in 1959.

It closed in 1990, reopened in 2005, became a cultural centre in 2008 and a Casa del Quartiere (community house) in 2015, with an active programme. That it was built as late as 1956 says how long many Turin homes lacked a bathroom.
An early-20th-century bathhouse in Nizza Millefonti, nicknamed "Barrito", where eight showers on the first floor still run for the public. It's one of the few that has never changed use.
It's a working service: respect the people who use it. The Vanchiglia baths are its better-known twin.

A low yellow building on Piazza Rebaudengo: the customs office of 1912, at the main northern goods entry into the city, still in its original form. It now houses a family centre and carries a 2017 mural of a flying ship by Alessandra Carloni.

Until 1930 goods entering Turin paid a municipal duty, the dazio, at a walled line. The first wall (1853) ran along today's ring of boulevards; the second (1912) was 23 km long, and its gates stood on big regular squares like this one, which is why the squares exist. Today's "Barriera di Milano" and "Barriera di Nizza" are named after those gates.
Other survivors: Piazza Stampalia 3, Piazza Cirene and Piazza Bengasi. One source says a post of the 1853 wall survives at Corso Moncalieri 80. Spot the yellow.
The 1912 toll quarters of the Barriera di Lanzo, built to the standard customs design and later enlarged. It's now a district meeting centre, one of four survivors of the customs wall.
Customs officers lived here with their families and checked every cart for wine, meat, flour and other taxed goods coming into the city. The wall was abolished in 1930.

The 1912 customs house on the Turin–Moncalieri border, at the old Barriera di Nizza. It was nearly demolished for the Metro 1 extension, then restored by 2023, with a new roof and the façade repainted in its original colours. Street-art panels were added when Bengasi metro station opened.
Its future use is still undecided. It's the newest-looking of the old toll houses, a good way to see what they looked like a century ago.
bengasi.s: MuseoTorino; Torino Oggi (2023). Map pin approximate

p: Inside the Mercato Centrale, the glass market hall at Porta Palazzo, two round 19th-century ice chambers are left open to view in a sunken plaza. You see their brick domes, sloping floors that drained the meltwater, and the hatches where ice was dropped in from above.

Before refrigerators, cities stored winter ice underground to keep food in summer. Maps from 1753 already show icehouses here, between Porta Palazzo and the Consolata. In winter, ice was cut from the frozen channels of the Dora and packed into chambers like these with straw; the street name Strada delle Ghiacciaie recalls the trade. Porta Palazzo, Europe's largest open-air market, depended on them.

They were found in 2002 while Massimiliano Fuksas's market hall was being built, and were kept as its centrepiece. Under Piazza Emanuele Filiberto, the 1845 Panizza icehouses at Via delle Orfane 32 spiral down about four levels and are still used by market vendors to store barrows; they're not open to the public.
The Mercato Centrale is free to enter in opening hours; the ground floor has been reorganised more than once, so check. Go through the Porta Palazzo market first.

A column by the Borgo Medievale entrance in the Valentino, marked with the heights reached by the Po's great floods. The highest is October 1839, at 6.20 metres. Stand next to it and look up: that is where the river was.

Turin sits where the Dora and other Alpine rivers join the Po, and autumn storms can raise it fast. In 1839 the Dora also swept away a bridge. The flood of October 2000 came within about 30 cm of the record, and that of November 2016 within about 50 cm. On 4 May 1949, the day of the Superga crash, the river rose to its fourth-highest mark.

It is the only flood marker in the city: none was found on the Murazzi, the riverside quays that flood most often. The Borgo Medievale behind it is itself a fake, a medieval village built for the 1884 exhibition.
Always visible. Walk along the river afterwards and you'll see how low the quays are.

A small museum of washerwomen in the parish courtyard of Bertolla, on Turin's north-eastern edge. Three rooms of washing tools, including the "scagn", the wooden box women knelt in at the river's edge, plus photos and costumes.

From about 1872 until the 1960s, Bertolla was Turin's laundry village. Families collected dirty laundry from the city's hotels and households, washed it in the Po and Stura rivers, and dried it on the meadows. A 1935 ban on drying laundry along the city rivers and then washing machines ended it.
Free, by appointment only (349 872 2649 in older sources).

A rack tramway that climbs 3.1 km from Sassi up to the basilica of Superga, at gradients of up to 21%, in wooden cars of 1934. Locals call it the "Dentiera", the dentures, for the toothed rack it grips. The ride takes about 18 minutes, through woods and over the city, and at the top is Juvarra's basilica.

It opened on 26 April 1884 on an unusual system invented by Tommaso Agudio: a steam engine at a fixed station drove a cable, and the train drew power from it. It was the only line of its kind, and GTT bills the line as unique in Italy. In 1934–35 it was converted to an electric rack, and the cars of that time still run. Motor car D2 has been restored in its original livery (2026), and Sassi station keeps a small history room in near-original condition.
Superga is a pilgrimage for two reasons: the basilica, built after the 1706 siege with the tombs of the Savoy kings, and the wall behind it where the Grande Torino died in 1949. Both are on this map.
Reopened on 3 April 2026. The summer timetable runs hourly 10:00–18:00 from Sassi, with no service on Wednesdays (a bus replaces it). Winter suspensions happen, so check gtt.to.it.

A single, very flat stone arch over the Dora: 45 metres of span with only 5.5 metres of rise. It's called unique among Europe's early 19th-century stone bridges. Seen from the riverside path, it looks impossibly thin for stone.

Napoleon ordered it in 1807, when Turin was a French provincial city, and it opened in 1830 under the restored Savoy kings. The engineer Carlo Bernardo Mosca was so confident that, the legend goes, he sat in a boat under it when the scaffolding came down, to prove it would hold. It was named after him only in 1868.
See it best from the riverside path. The old Torino–Ceres terminus is just north, and Porta Palazzo is a short walk.

The 1869 terminus of the Lanzo Valleys railway on Corso Giulio Cesare, by Ponte Mosca, disused since June 1986. It's a small station building with the air of a country station in the middle of the city.
The line carried people and goods from the Alpine valleys north of Turin to the city's markets. When the line was diverted, this terminus was abandoned. Outside only.

On the side wall of the cathedral, facing the passage to the Piazzetta Reale, a vertical noon line is painted with the signs of the zodiac, Capricorn at the top and Cancer at the bottom. A star-shaped hole above acts as the gnomon. At solar noon its spot of light falls on the line, at a height that tells you the season.

Before clocks were reliable, meridian lines set the city's noon, and churches were the natural place for them. The cathedral itself, dedicated to St John the Baptist, is Turin's only Renaissance church (1491–98); behind its altar is the chapel built to hold the Shroud.
Esoteric guides read the zodiac as an anti-Church code; a sundial specialist calls it a perfectly normal and correct meridian. Go around solar noon: about 12:20 in winter, 13:20 in summer.
meridiana.s: Roberto Baggio (gnomonist); general history. Map pin approximate

p: Seven torèt in a semicircle on Via Stradella. Torèt, "little bulls", are Turin's green cast-iron drinking fountains, each with a bull's-head spout: the bull is the city's emblem and its name (Toro, Torino). The city has about 800 of them.

The first was installed in 1862 under a plan to put clean water in every street. Turin people know the trick: press a finger on the spout and the water shoots up out of a hole on top, so you can drink. They run all year.
Other variants: the "lovers", two torèt facing each other at Via Stampatori 4, and a lioness-headed one in Parco della Pellerina. These rest on a single guide source.

torobrass.t: Brass bull of Piazza San Carlo
p: A brass rearing bull set into the pavement of the western arcade of Piazza San Carlo, near Caffè Torino. Step on its testicles with your heel and spin round once for luck. The worn hole tells you how many people do it.

The bull is Turin's emblem, a pun on the city's name. The ritual is pure folklore, but it's become as obligatory for visitors as throwing a coin in Rome's Trevi fountain. The Caval ëd Bronz with its bullet dent is in the middle of the same square.

Under the Prefettura arcade on Piazza Castello, students rub the little finger of a bronze Christopher Columbus before exams for luck, and it shines. But the monument isn't about Columbus. It's Dino Somà's 1923 memorial to the Italians from Latin America who came back to fight in the First World War; Columbus, as the link between Italy and the Americas, is only a medallion below the infantryman.

Thousands of Italian emigrants in Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay crossed the ocean to enlist. A historian of emigration called the finger ritual "a banal amulet" that has erased their story. The finger is said to have been replaced from wear.
ditocolombo.s: Emilio Franzina; GuidaTorino. Map pin approximate

p: At the west end of Piazza Statuto, a fountain topped by a pyramid of real rocks dug out of the Frejus rail tunnel, with marble Titans falling from it and a winged bronze figure on top. It was inaugurated in 1879 to celebrate the tunnel and its engineers, Germain Sommeiller, Severino Grandis and Sebastiano Grattoni.

The Frejus (or Mont Cenis) tunnel, 13.7 km under the Alps, opened in 1871 and was the first great Alpine rail tunnel. To dig it, Sommeiller invented a compressed-air rock drill, and the work went from both ends and met in the middle. It linked Turin to France and made the city a railway gateway.

The winged figure is the Genius of Science, not "Lucifer" as the black-magic tours claim. Its sculptor, Luigi Belli, later disowned the work. An inscription for the workers, many of whom died, was only added in 1971.
frejus.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026; general history

p: A carved wooden door of 1675, made in Paris, on Palazzo Trucchi di Levaldigi at the corner of Via XX Settembre and Via Alfieri, with a gilded knocker: a devil's head held by two snakes. Turin calls it the "Portone del Diavolo", the devil's door.

The palace has been a bank since 1939; in 1738 a factory for tarot cards was licensed here, which feeds the legends. Ghost stories tell of a dancer walled up inside and an officer who vanished; there's no evidence for any of them.
On the same corner look for the "Horns of Pan" mask, and more masks at the regional council entrance, Via Alfieri 15. Turin has over 200 such masks on its façades.

Turin's first skyscraper, an 87-metre rationalist tower of 1933–34 at the corner of Piazza Castello and Via Roma, clad in stone and brick. It was meant to be the Fascist party headquarters, the "Torre Littoria", and locals called it "the Duce's finger".

Via Roma was rebuilt in the 1930s as a Fascist showpiece, and this tower was its exclamation mark. The insurer Reale Mutua took it instead of the party. It carried an air-raid siren in the war. From the little square with the news kiosk you can see where the design changed during building. The city's own plaque on it gives the wrong dates.
It's offices; look from the street. The Torre BBPR, another Reale Mutua tower, is in Piazza Statuto.

toro.t: T'oro: bull bursting from a wall
p: Half a bull with golden horns smashing out of a brick wall on Via delle Orfane, with a scarab nearby: *T'oro*, a pun on toro (bull) and oro (gold), by the Turin artist Richi Ferrero. The bull is Turin's emblem.

Ferrero does light and street installations around the city. He also made the futurist gate at Via Lagrange 12, which shows a motorbike's movement in wrought iron (visible when the courtyard is open). The Consolata and Al Bicerin are a minute away.
toro.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026. Map pin approximate

p: In the courtyard passage of Palazzo Villa, between Piazza San Carlo and Via Lagrange, a big red head of David hangs upside down: a work by Andrea Salvatori that plays on Kant's famous line, turned round as "the starry sky within me, the moral law above me".
It's one of several contemporary pieces hidden in Turin's courtyards and passages. Look up as you walk through.
david.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026. Map pin approximate

p: An iron bench in the rock garden of the Valentino park where two street lamps sit side by side, one leaning its head on the other's shoulder, with a cat nearby: Rodolfo Marasciuolo's "lamps in love" (2002). Still there in February 2026.
It's become a spot for couples' photos. The Valentino itself was Turin's great 19th-century park, along the Po, with the castle, the botanic garden and the fake medieval village.
lampioni.s: Report on Turin's pass-by sights, Oct 2026. Map pin approximate

p: The central section of a real submarine, sitting in the Valentino park by the river. The *Andrea Provana* was a training submarine of 1915–18. After an accidental explosion in 1927, its middle section was shown at the 1928 Turin Expo and placed here in 1933 as a monument to the navy.
A submarine in a city 150 km from the sea is the joke. Only one guide source describes it, so check it's still there.

Look up at Via Madama Cristina 19 in San Salvario: two large stone bats hang under the third-floor balconies of this 1876 building. San Salvario was built in the 1850s–80s as a respectable new district, and builders competed with odd decorations. Single source.

A square of about 17 by 13 metres, with its own street sign and house number, at the corner of Via Cavour and Via Carlo Alberto, in front of the church of the Madonna degli Angeli. It was left over when the church was remodelled in 1901.

Cavour's funeral was held in this church on 7 June 1861, the day after his death in his house nearby; huge crowds filled the streets. The square is often called the smallest in Italy; that's disputed, and the city treats it as part of the neighbouring piazzetta.
Cavour's birth-and-death house is a minute away.
piazzetta.s: TorinoToday; Piemonte Go. Map pin approximate

p: Via Ercole Ricotti, between Corso Regina Margherita and Lungo Dora Siena, is Turin's shortest street: 23–30 metres, with only two house numbers on two mirror-image buildings. You can walk its whole length in ten steps.

Turin's centre is a Roman grid, so streets are mostly long and straight. The narrowest, vicolo Santa Maria in the medieval Quadrilatero, is 2.85 metres. The longest is Corso Regina Margherita (about 7.7 km), the widest Corso Salvemini (127.5 m).
ricotti.s: Atlante di Torino. Map pin approximate

p: Nothing to see, but stand on this corner: from 1379 to 1801 the city's civic tower rose here, with a gilded bull on its spire and Turin's first public clock (1387). It was the symbol of the commune, the city's self-government, as opposed to the duke's castle.
Napoleon's administration demolished it on 10 May 1801 to straighten Via Garibaldi, the old Roman main street. An old source says part of its east wall survives in Via Genova; unverified.

tours.name: Sieges, science and the guillotine: 18th-century Turin
tours.intro: In 1706 a French army besieged Turin; its shot is still in the walls and its tunnels under the Cittadella. The century that followed measured the meridian, opened the cafés and ended with a French guillotine in Piazza Carlina.
tours.how: On foot, west to east across the old centre. Book the Pietro Micca tunnels ahead.

stops.note: The 1564 keep, the only part of the Cittadella that held out in 1706 and still stands.
The counter-mine galleries where Pietro Micca fired the mine on the night of 29–30 August 1706.
Beccaria measured his geodetic baseline from here in 1760; the obelisk went up in 1808.
Open since 1763, opposite the Consolata.
Iron shot from 1706, and from the 1799 fighting over the Cittadella, walled in as memorials.
A pharmacy in the same family since 1682.
Trading since 1667; a bronze mortar of 1718.
The Academy of Sciences: its roof held Turin's first real observatory (1790); Lagrange was a founder.
Opened 1757, the oldest of the grand restaurants.
Guarini's baroque palace, later Italy's first parliament.
Founded 1780, the conservative café.
Under French rule (1798–1814) the guillotine stood here; 423 executions are reported.

story: The century opens with the siege of 1706: 117 days, a war fought partly underground in the counter-mine galleries, and Pietro Micca's mine. The shot fired into the city was later walled into façades as memorials.
Peace built a capital of science and cafés: Beccaria's meridian baseline (1760), the Academy of Sciences and its observatory, Del Cambio, Al Bicerin, Fiorio.
It closes with the French: from 1798 Piazza Carlina became the Place de la Liberté and its guillotine.

tours.name: Cavour's capital: the Risorgimento
tours.intro: Turin was Italy's first capital. From the gallows square to the hall where the Kingdom was proclaimed in 1861 and the night soldiers fired on the crowd in 1864.
tours.how: On foot from Valdocco to Piazza San Carlo; Al Bicerin closes on Wednesdays.

stops.note: Public hangings were held here 1835–1853; Cafasso accompanied 57 condemned men.
Cavour is said to have drunk here waiting for the royal family to leave the Consolata.
26 April 1852: the powder magazine blew up and Sergeant Sacchi kept 40,000 kg of powder from following.
Founded by Carlo Alberto in 1831–37.
Rattazzi, D'Azeglio, Balbo and Cavour were regulars; the Whist Club story is tradition.
The 1861 hall where the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed.
Cavour's table, marked with a plaque, facing the parliament.
The patriots' café, closed several times on suspicion of subversion.
22 September 1864: protests against moving the capital to Florence; the bullet dent is on the plinth.
Cavour was born and died in this house (1810, 1861).

story: Turin was the first capital of united Italy, proclaimed in 1861 in Palazzo Carignano. The men of unification lived within a few streets: Cavour's table at Del Cambio, the patriots at Caffè San Carlo, the conservatives at Fiorio.

The period had its violence: the gallows at the Rondò until 1853, the 1852 powder-magazine explosion in Borgo Dora, and on 21–22 September 1864 cadets firing on crowds protesting the move of the capital to Florence; the dent is still on the Caval ëd Bronz.

tours.name: Belle Époque: cinema, cars and public baths
tours.intro: Between the 1884 rack tram and the 1912 customs wall, Turin became Italy's film capital and its car city, and built public baths for workers' housing without bathrooms.
tours.how: A transit day: centre on foot, then tram and bus to the edges.

stops.note: 7 November 1896: Calcina's Lumière show, often billed as Italy's first; Milan had one on 29 March 1896.
A Lumière room opened in this arcade's basement in 1905.
Torino FC was founded on the mezzanine on 3 December 1906.
Fiat's founding deed was signed here in July 1899.
Dolza's Liberty bathhouse, frogs and shells on the cornice.
Fiat's first plant, 1899–1900.
Lancia founded at this corner on 27 November 1906.
1901 baths, still working.
Fenoglio's 1911–13 studio for Italy's biggest silent-film company.
The chimney of Michelin's first Italian plant (1906).
The 1912 customs-wall toll house, original form.
The 1884 Sassi–Superga line, rack since 1935.

story: Turin lost the capital in 1865 and reinvented itself: by 1914 Ambrosio and Itala made it Italy's film capital, and Fiat (1899) and Lancia (1906) its car city.
The 1908 plan put public baths in the workers' districts; several still sell showers. In 1912 a new customs wall ringed the city, and its yellow toll houses still stand on the big 'barrier' squares.

tours.name: Fascism and the bombs
tours.intro: From the squads of 1922 to the raids of 1940–45: the massacre plaque, the Fascist tower, the shelters and the ruins the bombs left.
tours.how: Mostly on foot in the centre; the Piazza Risorgimento shelter is a tram ride and opens only on special dates.

stops.note: 18–20 December 1922: Brandimarte's squads killed 11 and burned the Camera del Lavoro.
A 1940 shelter for town-hall staff, original doors and signs.
The 1933–34 tower meant as the Fascist HQ, 'il dito del Duce'.
The former Casa del Littorio, seat of the Fascist federation; the "Campana" partisan brigade occupied it on 28 April 1945.
A whole block, the old Politecnico, bombed away.
Gutted on 8 December 1942: the city's only conspicuous visible war ruin.
Eight shelter mouths in the hill, six bricked up.
The 21 November 1942 raid gutted the interior; the towers survived.
One of the big public shelters, three concrete galleries 12 m down.

story: Fascism arrived in Turin with the December 1922 massacre. The regime left the Torre Littoria on Piazza Castello and the Casa del Littorio (now Palazzo Campana).
From June 1940 the city was bombed; only 15% of the population had a safe shelter. The Teatro di Torino ruin and the Valdo Fusi void are what remains to see above ground.

tours.name: Occupation and Resistance
tours.intro: September 1943 to April 1945: the prison, the firing range, the street executions, the deportations and the insurrection.
tours.how: Spread out: tram between the centre stops; Pian del Lot needs a car.

stops.note: Le Nuove held political and Jewish prisoners; its shelter is 18 m down.
About sixty partisans shot by RSI squads; 59 names on the plaque.
Nine partisans shot on this spot on 12 October 1944.
Factory plaques from the April 1945 insurrection.
Five worker-partisans fell here under tank fire on 27 April 1945.
The Valabrega stones: deported on Primo Levi's convoy.
Political deportees left from this station.
27 prisoners from Le Nuove shot on 2 April 1944.

story: After September 1943 Le Nuove filled with political and Jewish prisoners; the Martinetto range and Pian del Lot were where many were shot.
The city rose on 26–28 April 1945; workers' squads fought from the factories, and their plaques survive at Cascina Marchesa and the Museo Diffuso.

tours.name: The Fiat century: factory, migrants and boom
tours.intro: Fiat shaped Turin and drew migrants from the south. Follow it from the rooftop test track to Italia '61 and the housing, churches and cemetery the boom made necessary.
tours.how: A day across the city by metro, tram and bus. Ivrea is a separate day trip.

stops.note: The 1920s plant: cars built floor by floor going up, tested on the roof.
The 1961 Alweg monorail, closed in 1963.
Nervi and Ponti's hall for Italia '61, now a fenced ruin.
The 1937–39 plant, 2 million m²; Porta 5 was the gate of the labour struggles.
Mosso's 1957 church in Mirafiori.
1960s towers for the growing south-west.
Built in 1969–72 because the Monumentale was full.
Vitellozzi's arena built with the Fiat design office for Italia '61.
71 ha of 1958–68 public housing for 20,000 people.
Astengo's 1950s INA-Casa village.
Prefab slabs for southern migrants drawn by Fiat.

story: In the 1920s Fiat built Lingotto, then in 1937–39 Mirafiori. The company drew workers from the south and the city grew around them: Falchera, the Vallette, Corso Taranto.
The boom's showpiece was Italia '61: Nervi's Palazzo del Lavoro, Vitellozzi's arena and the monorail that ran for two years.

off.note: The other industrial dream: Olivetti's Ivrea.

tours.name: The years of lead
tours.intro: Riots, firebombs, a newspaperman shot in his doorway, the march that broke the Fiat strike, and the cinema fire that changed Italy's safety law.
tours.how: Centre stops on foot; Mirafiori by bus.

stops.note: 3 July 1969: the Corso Traiano riot by Gate 2. No plaque.
16 November 1977: the Red Brigades shot Carlo Casalegno in this doorway.
14 October 1980: the supervisors' march that ended the 35-day strike.
1 October 1977: a firebomb killed the student Roberto Crescenzio.
13 February 1983: 64 died behind chained exits.

story: From the Corso Traiano riot of 1969 to the Red Brigades' first murder of a journalist in 1977, Turin was at the centre of Italy's years of lead.
The period closed with the 'march of the 40,000' in 1980 and, in 1983, the Cinema Statuto fire.

tours.name: After Fiat: Olympics, ruins and reuse
tours.intro: When the factories closed, Turin reused some sites, staged the 2006 Olympics and left others to rot.
tours.how: City stops by metro, tram and bus; the Olympic sites are a mountain day by car.

stops.note: Renzo Piano's conversion; the track is now a garden.
The 2006 Olympic arch and footbridge.
The one not saved.
Nervi's hall restored as the central library, opening 11 Dec 2026.
Grandi Motori, being demolished since 2025.
The sunken rail corridor, Metro 2 from 2027.
The sneaker plant, abandoned 1998, becoming a culture hub.
Botta's church on the old steelworks, the chimney kept as a bell tower.
The December 2007 fire killed seven workers.

story: As industry left, its sites were reused: Lingotto, Parco Dora, soon the Trincerone. Others stand fenced: ThyssenKrupp, OGM, the Palazzo del Lavoro.
The 2006 Winter Olympics left an arch and an athletes' village in the city and two ruins in the mountains.

off.note: The 2006 bobsleigh track, funded for demolition.
The 2006 ski jumps, matting falling apart.

tours.name: Nervi, Vitellozzi and the great concrete halls
tours.intro: Nervi's two Turin halls, one reborn and one rotting, with Vitellozzi's arena and Fiat's factory.
tours.how: Along the river and Via Nizza by metro; the PalaRuffini is a bus ride west.

stops.note: Vitellozzi's own favourite, twin of his Rome Palazzetto.
The 1948–50 ferrocement vault, the 'cattedrale moderna'.
The concrete factory with a test track on the roof.
Sixteen concrete 'mushroom' columns under steel umbrellas.

story: Nervi roofed Salone B in 1948–50 and built the Palazzo del Lavoro with Ponti for 1961; Vitellozzi's PalaRuffini is the same year's other great roof.

tours.name: Mollino and the Neoliberty
tours.intro: Turin's own modernism: Mollino's opera house and offices, and the Neoliberty of Gabetti & Isola and Jaretti & Luzi.
tours.how: Centre stops on foot; Torri Pitagora by bus. Lago Nero is a mountain day.

stops.note: Mollino's largest work, inside Juvarra's façade.
Gabetti & Isola's early trading hall, closed since 1992.
Mollino's offices on a central core, with his helical stair.
Jaretti & Luzi's oyster-door provocation.
Jaretti & Luzi's forest of pillars.

story: Carlo Mollino left Turin the Teatro Regio and the Palazzo degli Affari; his sled station at Lago Nero is the mountain coda.
The Neoliberty generation answered rationalism with curves and craft: the Borsa, the Casa dell'Obelisco, Torri Pitagora.

tours.name: Concrete churches and a landscape cemetery
tours.intro: Post-conciliar Turin built churches in concrete for the new estates. Some are confirmed exposed concrete; the rest need your eyes.
tours.how: A transit day; Moriondo, Nichelino and Piossasco by car.

stops.note: Mosso's faceted concrete vault (1955–57).
The bell tower that dominates the skyline.
Bardelli's church with a gym in the undercroft.
A pointed 'cuspide' roof.
Bianco's all-concrete central plan with a floating roof.
Botta's towers and a steelworks chimney.
Hillocks hiding the concrete burial blocks.
Mosso's pentagon of six pillars, the Redentore's sibling.
Beams knitting into a net, modelled on the Redentore.
Roggero among the Mirafiori Sud estates.
A church made of factory-shed parts for Fiat Rivalta workers.

story: Under Cardinal Pellegrino (1965–77) the diocese built dozens of churches for the migrant estates. Mosso's Redentore set the type; Gabetti & Isola's Piossasco church is its most famous child.
Exposed concrete is confirmed for some, not all: the 'plausible' tags mark the ones to check in person.

tours.name: Industrial ruins and fenced giants
tours.intro: The fenced carcasses of industrial Turin, seen from the street.
tours.how: A bus day; everything is exterior only. Don't trespass.

stops.note: Nervi's abandoned hall.
Coachbuilding plant, abandoned 2001.
1911–52 asbestos factory.
The 2007 fire site.
Sneaker plant, abandoned 1998.
One chimney left.
The Ceres terminus, disused since 1986.
Grandi Motori's Basilica hall on a demolition site.
The overgrown rail trench.

story: Turin's industrial decline left giants behind; most are fenced, some are being demolished or converted. See them now.

tours.name: Nietzsche's last autumn, and the legends
tours.intro: Nietzsche lived here for four months and collapsed in the street on 3 January 1889. This tour keeps fact and legend apart.
tours.how: On foot in the old centre.

stops.note: His lodging: fourth floor, fifth window from the corner.
The ice-cream link is the least weak café claim.
A blog says he 'certainly' came; nothing supports it.
Piazza Carlo Alberto, where most sources place the horse story.
His name is on the wall, by tradition only.

story: Nietzsche lodged at Via Carlo Alberto 6 from September 1888, wrote Ecce Homo there and collapsed on 3 January 1889. The horse story is disputed; the café claims mostly legend.

tours.name: Writers' Turin: Rousseau to Primo Levi
tours.intro: Where writers lived, sat and died: Rousseau's abjuration, Pavese's café and hotel room, Primo Levi's house.
tours.how: On foot; Caffè Elena and Al Bicerin close on Wednesdays.

stops.note: Rousseau abjured Calvinism here in April 1728, aged 16.
Umberto Eco set a scene of The Prague Cemetery here.
A 1920s literary circle; the Gramsci line is marketing.
Pavese spent his time writing here; the Comune says so.
Pavese was found dead in room 346 on 27 August 1950.
Pavese, Einaudi and Ginzburg, per popular sources.
Primo Levi's birth and death house.

story: From Rousseau's months as a convert and footman to Pavese and Primo Levi, Turin's writers are easier to place than its philosophers.

tours.name: Gramsci and the red city
tours.intro: Gramsci's lodging and newspaper, the 1920 factory occupations, workers' clubs and the 1922 reprisal.
tours.how: Centre on foot; Fiat Corso Dante and Mirafiori by bus.

stops.note: L'Ordine Nuovo was written in these rooms.
December 1922: the squads burned the Camera del Lavoro.
The 1957 plaque: Gramsci lived at no. 15 in 1919–21.
A still-active workers' mutual-aid club.
Hub of the September 1920 occupations.
Porta 5, gate of the 1970s struggles.

story: Gramsci lived on Piazza Carlina in 1919–21 and wrote L'Ordine Nuovo, the paper of the factory councils that occupied Fiat in September 1920. The squads' reply came in December 1922.

tours.name: Science Turin: the meridian, nitroglycerine and Lombroso
tours.intro: Beccaria's measured baseline, Sobrero's lab, the old observatory, Lagrange, the induction motor, and the museums of anatomy and criminology.
tours.how: Centre on foot, then tram to the Valentino; Rivoli is a separate trip.

stops.note: The Turin end of the 1760 meridian baseline.
A noon line on the cathedral wall.
The city observatory, 1822–1912.
Beccaria taught physics here; the 1904 fire burned the manuscripts.
Nitroglycerine, first made in the lab here (1846–47).

story: Turin measured the Earth (Beccaria, 1760), made nitroglycerine (Sobrero, 1847) and the rotating magnetic field (Ferraris, 1885). Lombroso's museum shows science gone wrong, which is why it matters.

story: Turin's small oddities sit close together, from Ferrero's bull to the smallest square. Most of the 'magic' stories attached to them are legend: see the myths tour.

story: Guides sell Turin as a corner of a black-magic triangle. The stops are real; the stories mostly are not. Each note says which part is record.

story: The customs walls of 1853 and 1912 made the 'barrier' districts; the baths of the 1900s served workers' flats without bathrooms; the Renzi firm cast urinals sold across Italy. Several survive.
